author: Malik Chiconela Santana
title: A judicial solution to a political problem
content:
Venâncio Bila Mondlane, the leader of the Mozambican opposition, finds himself awaiting trial (scheduled for November 17) for his alleged role as the progenitor of the seismic protests that followed the 2024 elections and threatened to topple the state. Mondlane is president of the recently formed National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (ANAMOLA) party. He is accused of five crimes by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, namely

public justification of crime, incitement of collective disobedience, public instigation of crime, instigation of terrorism, and incitement of terrorism

. A conviction could mean up to 20 years in prison for the presidential runner-up, the crippling of the opposition, and a transition in the state’s handling of political opponents.

Mondlane’s road to the 2024 ballot was lined with legal and procedural obstacles.

Blocked

 from contesting the leadership of his party at the time, the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO), he left it and allied his campaign with the Democratic Alliance Coalition (CAD), whose electoral eligibility was confirmed on May 9, but was excluded by the National Election Commission (CNE) on July 18. The Constitutional Council (CC) upheld the decision on appeal, arguing that the parties who had formed CAD failed to notify the

Ministry of Justice and Constitutional and Religious Matters

 of their intention to form a coalition. The court framed the decision as a purely technical issue; however, its consequences were undeniably political. Mondlane found himself politically isolated only two months before the elections. Forced to reorganize his campaign, Mondlane forged a last-minute partnership with the Optimistic People for the Development of Mozambique (PODEMOS), running as an independent with the party’s political and parliamentary support.

This chronology illustrates how the political agency of Mondlane and his supporters was repeatedly at odds with applications of the electoral law. It may not establish that each application of electoral law was politically motivated, but, at the very least, it raises a broader question of how ostensibly procedural outcomes can reshape the field of political competition, and suggests that legal procedure is not necessarily neutral.

After the October 9, 2024, vote, the CNE declared Daniel Chapo, candidate of the ruling Mozambique Liberation Front (Frelimo), the winner with about 70%, to Mondlane’s 20%. In December, after more than 300 complaints of electoral crimes and irregularities had been lodged with local and district courts, the Constitutional Council revised those figures to roughly 65% and 24% respectively. The revision was, in effect, an admission that the election commission’s results were dubious at best and fictional at worst. The CC altered the results when, as a body of electoral oversight, it could only order the CNE to recount the votes or annul the elections. Unsurprisingly,

the Mozambican Bar Association

 (OAM), opposition parties, and civil society groups expressed concerns over the CC’s vague legal reasoning and the lack of an evidentiary basis for its alteration of the results.

What ensued in the wake of these opaque elections was a six-month period of unprecedented violence. In Mozambique, several elections have been followed by periods of armed conflict. What made this period unprecedented, however, was that the antagonism was not between the state and an organized army, but rather between the state and a mobilized mass of unarmed civilians. According to a

report

 by the Mozambican NGO Plataforma Decide, 411 civilians were killed, some 3,700 were injured, and around 7,200 were illegally detained between October 2024 and January 2025. These figures were disputed by the then commander-general of the police, Bernardino Rafael, who stated that 96 civilians were killed. Even so, charges have only been brought

against two officers

, and, with no updates, it is unclear whether the prosecution is pursuing these cases at all.

The protests began on October 21, when Mondlane called for a peaceful march in tribute to Elvino Dias, his lawyer, who was assassinated by assailants of no particular origin as he prepared an appeal challenging the preliminary election results. This march, like many that followed, was dispersed violently, including through the use of tear gas and live ammunition. In an environment where constitutionally protected political activities are met with violence, the credibility of …

author: Nelly Madegwa
title: Pregnancy in a Warming Africa
content:
At 8:30 a.m., Stella is usually already at the Kakamega Forest dispensary in Kakamega County, western Kenya, for her antenatal care (ANC) appointment. Seven months pregnant, she has learnt to organise her household around the rising heat, doing most of her chores when temperatures are lower.


The clinic is 2.5 kilometres away, a distance she walks. Arriving early allows her to complete her check-ups and begin the journey home before the sun becomes unbearable.


Her routine reflects a change that Doreen Atamba, a community health promoter who has supported expectant mothers for the past ten years, has observed among women attending the facility. Increasingly, expectant mothers arrive between 8 a.m. and 10 a.m., with fewer coming after 10 a.m. By late morning, attendance drops considerably.


Atamba says the heat is affecting not only when women seek antenatal care but also their comfort and well-being at home. Some expectant mothers complain that intense temperatures make everyday activities difficult and disrupt their sleep.


“Some of them tell me they are really struggling with the heat, even at night when they are trying to sleep,” she says.


To help them cope, Atamba encourages pregnant women to wear loose-fitting clothing, drink plenty of water, avoid unnecessary exposure to extreme heat, rest frequently and seek relief in cooler places, especially shaded areas.


These everyday adjustments are taking place amid rising temperatures and growing concern about the effects of climate change on maternal and newborn health.


Across Africa, experts in Kenya, South Africa, Senegal and Nigeria are increasingly concerned about how climate-related extremes are affecting pregnant women and newborns. Extreme heat can cause dehydration and physical strain, while drought, flooding, food insecurity and disrupted healthcare services can compound the risks. Experts say the consequences depend not only on the weather but also on women’s living and working conditions, access to water and nutrition, and the ability of health facilities to provide safe care.


Heat and pregnancy


Pregnancy places additional demands on the body. During extreme heat, dehydration and the effort required to regulate body temperature can put additional strain on the heart and circulatory system. Researchers are still investigating how this stress may affect the placenta and developing baby.


Ijeoma Solarin, a senior researcher at Wits Planetary Health Research, and Kimberly McAlpine, a medical student and PhD researcher at Wits University, point to growing evidence associating high temperatures with preterm birth, stillbirth, low birth weight and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.


A 2025

study

 by Carrie Ngongo and colleagues, analysing 22.7 million births in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, found that each 1°C increase in temperature above 34°C was associated with an additional 2.3 stillbirths per 1,000 births and 27.3 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.


A separate

study

 at a Johannesburg hospital linked high temperatures early in pregnancy to approximately 1.8 times the risk of severe hypertensive disorders, including pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.


Research

 involving pregnant subsistence farmers in The Gambia has also documented signs of fetal distress during hot weather, including unusual changes in the baby’s heart rate and increased resistance to blood flow through the umbilical cord, which supplies oxygen and nutrients from the placenta.


The scale of concern extends beyond individual studies. A

Wellcome-commissioned poll

 of 1,001 healthcare professionals in Australia, Brazil, India, the United Kingdom and Zimbabwe found that 98 per cent had cared for a pregnant woman whose health they believed had been adversely affected by extreme heat. Meanwhile, 99 per cent reported caring for a baby whose health they believed had been adversely affected by extreme heat.


These findings reflect healthcare professionals’ reported experiences and perceptions, rather than estimates of the proportion of pregnant women or babies experiencing medically confirmed heat-related harm. Nevertheless, they highlight concerns among health workers about the effects of extreme heat on mothers and babies.


As climate change drives more frequent and intense heat extremes, exposure to dangerous temperatures is becoming an increasing health risk. However, this risk is not experienced equally. Social and economic inequalities mean some women have …

author: Carla Habif
title: How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win
content:
This article

How Brazilians pulled off Lula’s surprise win

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Oct. 25, Brazilians made history by resisting hopelessness and achieving, for the first time since the return to democracy in 1985, a comeback in the runoff of a presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection by more than 4 million votes after losing the first round to opponent Flávio Bolsonaro by over 2 million votes.


Lula, a former metalworker and union leader who co-founded the left-wing Workers’ Party,

was seeking his fourth term as president. Flávio, by contrast, was the candidate of the far-right Liberal Party and was running as the successor to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally who was

convicted and imprisoned for attempting a coup d’état

.


The first round suggested that Flávio and his party were on track to gain an enormous amount of power. The party won

more seats in Congress than any other


—

 nearly a quarter of the lower house and more than a third of the Senate — which, together with other right-wing parties,

gave the right a majority in both houses

.


Two days after the vote,

Flávio said he would use that majority to “change the Constitution” and “re-democratize” the country. Asked what he meant, he

proposed

 limiting the powers of Supreme Court justices, lowering the age of criminal responsibility and ending presidential reelection, and he left open the possibility of extending the presidential term from four to five years.


“I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


In addition, whoever won in October would be able to

appoint up to four of the 11 justices of the federal Supreme Court

,

the same court that convicted Jair Bolsonaro. A Flávio victory would have given the far right control over all three branches of government, amid the advance of the far right in Latin America and the United States.


As a result, after the first-round results came in on

the night of Oct. 4, the mood among Lula’s supporters was one of deep discouragement and fear. But this fear quickly turned into forms of popular organizing that were diverse, complementary and consistently nonviolent — and they changed the course of the race. The mobilizations included a large-scale effort by politicians, activists, content creators and ordinary supporters to organize and amplify pro-Lula content on social media, and an equally massive occupation of the country’s streets in peaceful demonstrations.


Students took center stage in the street mobilizations, with thousands turning out for protests such as one

led by the National Union of Students, or UNE, at the Candelária

 church in Rio de Janeiro, and one led by UNE and the University of Brasília’s student council on the Esplanade of Ministries in Brasília. People in the streets and on social media acted together and complemented each other.


Beyond protests and online activism, people organized to make sure that those who had not voted in the first round would go to the polls, including elderly people and those who live far from their polling places. They also got off the internet and talked in person with undecided voters who had not yet made up their minds, a process that had a name: vira voto, or flip the vote.


For Gabriel Rochlin,

a director, actor and teacher who took part in a vira voto group in Rio de Janeiro, this was a way to get out of the social media bubble. “The work of vira voto has a lot to do with breaking through the algorithm,” he said. “The street has this real quality of not having an algorithm that separates people: you’re going to meet people you would never meet on your feed.” He saw the fear engendered by the first round as the turning point: “I really think the desperation and fear after the first round changed everything. There was a need to act with more urgency, and this desire to organize.”


From demoralization to esperançar


Given the collective feeling of fear and hopelessness after the first round of voting, the first challenge was to shift the mood of the left. It was on Oct. 5, the day after the results, that popular mobilization began in earnest.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Award-winning Mary Paningajak sees art as a way to heal
content:
Mary Paningajak grew up surrounded by art in Ivujivik.


She watched her father, Tivi Paningajak, make prints and sculptures, and she remembers visiting his studio.


“One time, he let me make a screen print,” Paningajak said in an interview Tuesday at Kuuujjuaq’s adult education centre.


She was nine years old when she first started making art and spent years learning different tools and techniques.


Now 65, her artistic practice has earned her northern Quebec’s artist of the year award from Quebec’s Council of Arts and Letters, or the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec. It’s a $15,000 prize that recognizes her contribution to Nunavik’s arts community.


The council’s director general Véronique Fontaine presented the award on Nov. 8, during the opening night of the Path to 100 festival in Kuujjuaq, which commemorates the anniversary of the signing of the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.


“I was so surprised to hear that I won because there are lots of artists in Canada and Quebec. I was thinking, how come they chose me?” Paningajak said in an interview.


Mary Paningajak demonstrates one of the printmaking techniques she taught participants at the Path to 100 festival, using a spoon to press an inked design onto paper in Kuujjuaq on Nov. 10. (Photo by Dominique Gené)


Working in printmaking, graphic arts and sculpture, she draws inspiration from Inuit history, personal experience and her community.


Pursuing art in Ivujivik, a community of about 412 people on the northern tip of the Ungava peninsula, comes with practical challenges.


“We only have one store, and it doesn’t have any art supplies inside. It’s hard to get materials because we have to travel south by plane or ask people to order things for us,” she said.


Despite those challenges, Paningajak’s work has been exhibited across Canada.


Sikutsajaq, 

a solo exhibition, inaugurated the Centre Sanaaq in Montreal in May 2025. 


Sharing her knowledge of art is also an important part of her work.


During Path to 100, Paningajak led a printmaking workshop, showing participants how to create prints using rubber plates.

Participants drew designs onto the plates, carved them into the rubber and rolled ink over the raised surfaces before transferring their images onto paper.


“I hope that what they learned, maybe some of them will be interested in making more art,” Paningajak said.


The festival invited artists and community members to reflect on Nunavik’s past and imagine what the next 50 years could look like.


For Paningajak, that future includes giving younger generations opportunities to express themselves and find healing through art.


She said making art has helped her work through trauma from past abuse.


“It was important to me to heal through the paper, and I want them to heal in any way they can in the future,” she said.

author: S. Baum
title: Justice Department Official Who Led Attacks on Gender-Affirming Care Resigns
content:
Brett Shumate is the fourth DOJ official to resign since the midterms after leading investigations that pressured hospitals to end care for trans minors.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Brett Shumate has become the fourth Department of Justice official to join the post-election exodus from the agency following Republicans’ crushing midterm defeat — marking the end of the tenure of a man who helped grease the wheels of the anti-trans machine.

“The rats are fleeing the sinking ship,” Alejandra Caraballo, a lawyer and trans rights scholar, posted on Bluesky, alongside news that Shumate, the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Division, was resigning.

Under Shumate’s leadership, the DOJ aggressively targeted providers of gender-affirming care, subpoenaing patient records and waging False Claims Act investigations to intimidate hospitals. This caused some major hospitals to end care for trans minors and pay millions in settlements to the government. He was also instrumental in defending these actions in court against claims they were unlawful government overreach.

No hospital or clinic has been successfully sued because it provides evidence-based medicine, but some of them signed agreements with the DOJ to stave off the worst of federal threats: the demand that providers hand over identifiable patient data about thousands of transgender children and their families. Not all of these investigations or deals have been public.

Still, hospitals shut down their gender-affirming care programs for trans youth, leaving care deserts across the country. Lower courts condemned the government’s ploy, with one Boston judge calling it “a fishing expedition.” In a similar Rhode Island case, another judge said the DOJ — under Shumate’s leadership at the time — “has proven unworthy of this trust at every point in this case.”

In June 2025, Shumate issued a memo directing Civil Division employees to prioritize attacks on gender-affirming care, courtesy of the whims of President Donald Trump and then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, who was ousted in April. Shumate’s memo announced the Civil Division will “prioritize investigations of doctors, hospitals, pharmaceutical companies, and other appropriate entities” that ostensibly violate Trump’s declarations about transgender youth care. “In addition, the Civil Division will aggressively pursue claims under the False Claims Act against health care providers that bill the federal government for impermissible services.”

This largely included providers of wholly legal gender-affirming care, even in blue states — such as Children’s Hospital Los Angeles in California and Mount Sinai Hospital in New York. There is no federal ban on gender-affirming care.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in announcing Shumate’s departure on X, praised him for “shutter[ing] dozens of clinics” for gender-affirming care.

The DOJ also saw the departure of Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division, and whose firm previously represented “ex-trans” activist Chloe Cole in her lawsuit against Kaiser Permanente for providing gender-affirming care.

Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the National Security Division, also resigned. The department is also reeling from general attrition of staff throughout. The DOJ is not likely to stop pursuing political targets, including trans people and their caretakers and doctors, but if nothing else, the turmoil at the DOJ is liable to make it less effective. Under Trump, “a drastically diminished Justice Department workforce is struggling to keep up with its civil side caseloads,” The Hill found.

“A series of charts, apparently inadvertently shared and then recalled, show how the number of attorneys within the civil division has plummeted under the Trump administration.” This may slow down some of the destructive efforts by the DOJ — going after lawful gender-affirming care providers, defending the government from lawsuits over human rights violations. But others question how this might shape the department politically as new hires grow increasingly conservative and less qualified or willing to defy unlawful orders. Other important targets of the DOJ, such as those guilty of terrorism or white-collar crime, may also benefit from less competence in oversight.

A replacement for Shumate has not yet been announced.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations
content:
First Nations Bank of Canada (FNBC) president and CEO Bill Lomax says the federal budget offers a rare opening for First Nations to move from consultation into genuine ownership of the infrastructure and energy projects that will define Canada’s economy for decades.


Lomax framed the scale of planned investments in transportation, energy and electricity infrastructure as “a generational opportunity for First Nations to play a leading role in building Canada’s future.”


“When First Nations move beyond participation to become owners, we create lasting economic opportunities, build wealth for future generations and strengthen Canada’s economy as a whole. When First Nations succeed, Canada succeeds,” Lomax said in a statement following the budget. 


“But we need to think beyond consultation, employment and contracting opportunities. While these remain important, First Nations must also be recognized as business partners and owners, with the ability to build businesses, acquire equity and participate directly in the long-term economic benefits these projects generate.”


The FNBC is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank, founded in 1996, operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.6 billion in assets, and through its subsidiary FNB Trust, administers approximately $5.5 billion.


The federal budget, tabled Nov. 5, commits more than $50 billion over 10 years to Indigenous programs and services. The largest single piece is $32 billion over a decade for First Nations housing and on-reserve infrastructure. 


That includes the new First Nations On-Reserve Infrastructure Program, backed by $18.5 billion for infrastructure and $11 billion for housing that aims to maintain, renovate and build thousands of homes over 10 years. 


“This budget is an opportunity to invest in who we are,” Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty told APTN News in an interview Tuesday. “It’s an opportunity to better define who we are. It’s an opportunity to have a strategic approach to what our financial position is going to be, and I think the greatest opportunity of all is to demonstrate to Canadians the fiscal impact that Indigenous people have on the Canadian economy.”


Indigenous Services Canada Minister Mandy Gull Masty at a news conference on Parliament Hill in May. Photo: APTN.


The budget also introduces the new Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) for Canadian entrepreneurs, investors and employees, which is also open to Indigenous business people. The goal of the CGI is to keep investment money in Canada. 


It offers a new capital gains tax exemption for “Canadian builders” of up to $15 million earned from the Canadian businesses they invested in. 

To benefit, Canadians will have to reinvest and keep their money in Canada and Canadian businesses.  


“The Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) will be one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada by creating the path for entrepreneurs, investors, and employees to reinvest in Canada,” the budget said. “This represents a level shift in the attractiveness of firms, large and small, to invest-and reinvest-in Canada, and deliver lasting prosperity for all Canadians.”  


The budget is also promising money for education, health, child welfare, policing and emergency management. 


The budget also outlines the government’s support for the Indigenous Loan Program that loans money to First Nations for projects. 


“I hope everybody listening or reading our interviews about the budget understands that I’m here to spend money; come to me with your proposals. I’m going to do everything I can to meet the needs, so work with me,” said Gull Masty. 


 Where’s the money?


Aaron Pete, chief of Chawathil First Nation in British Columbia, told APTN that he’s taking a cautious approach to the budget because the money “rarely finds its way to First Nation communities in a constructive way.” 


Chief of Chawathil First Nation Aaron Pete. Photo From aaronpete.com,


“It [the budget] sounds promising, but again, my concern is that it gets stuck in Ottawa and doesn’t actually reach these communities,” he said. 


Pete was a councillor in 2022 and became chief in 2025. He has a podcast where politicians of all stripes are invited to share their opinions on the state of the country and First Nations politics. 


He acknowledged that many of the government’s stated priorities — clean running water …

author: FMF Staff
title: Aisha Wahab’s Victory Shows What Afghan Women Can Achieve. The Taliban Is Denying Afghanistan That Future.
content:
Last week, amid the many historic firsts and important victories in the midterm elections, Afghan American Aisha Wahab won her first full term representing California’s 14th District.

Wahab’s victory is a powerful reminder of what women can accomplish when given the opportunity to lead. Her commitment to public service reflects the talent, determination, and leadership Afghan women bring to their communities and to the world.

At a time when women and girls in Afghanistan are systematically excluded from public life, her achievement is also a reminder of what Afghanistan is losing by denying its women the opportunity to serve, lead, and shape their country’s future.

The contrast could not be more striking.

Wahab’s achievement should not be exceptional. Women’s leadership should be the norm, not the exception. Yet women’s opportunities to lead are still too often denied, obstructed, or dismissed.

Afghan women are just as capable of serving their communities, shaping policy, and holding public office as women anywhere in the world. They have the knowledge, ambition, and commitment. What they need is the opportunity.

The Taliban has made that opportunity impossible for women and girls in Afghanistan. Since returning to power in August 2021, it has barred girls from education beyond the sixth grade, excluded women from universities and most employment, and systematically erased women from public life by issuing over 160 decrees. These restrictions are not simply a collection of discriminatory policies. They are part of a system designed to deny women autonomy, human rights, and participation in society. In other words, it’s a system of gender apartheid.

And Afghanistan is paying the price.

When women are excluded from public service, the country loses leaders who could work for its people. When women are denied education, the country loses future teachers, doctors, scientists, advocates, and policymakers. When women are forced out of the workforce, families, communities, and the national economy suffer. The Taliban’s oppression of women is not only a violation of their rights; it is an assault on Afghanistan’s future.

Aisha Wahab’s victory makes visible what the Taliban seeks to suppress: Afghan women’s capacity to lead, contribute, and shape the world around them.

Her story is a reminder that women’s rights have never been a question of capability or merit. They are a matter of policy, equality and opportunity. The barriers are not a reflection of what women can achieve, but of the systems designed to deny them the chance.

The world must not forget the women and girls of Afghanistan. Their exclusion must not become normalized, and their struggle must not fade from the global agenda. Leaders, governments and institutions must continue to demand an end to the Taliban’s system of gender apartheid and stand for Afghan women’s fundamental rights to education, employment, and full participation in society.

An Afghanistan that excludes its women cannot fulfill its potential. And a world that celebrates women’s achievements while forgetting those denied the chance to achieve is failing them too.

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: smǝlqmíx Youth lead rally against greenlit Copper Mountain Mine expansion: ‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’
content:
smǝlqmíx Youth and members of the nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders stand together at a gathering that they led in Keremeos on Nov. 8, where they continued to voice their opposition to the nearby Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle Expansion project. From left to right: Chase Dennis, Isaac Dennis, Madeline Terbasket, Meadow Arcand, Kirsten Lindley, and Coven Terbasket.

 Photo by Aaron Hemens


A group of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) Youth are continuing calls to stop a controversial mine expansion project in their homelands after it was greenlit by the province earlier this year. 


Members of the nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders, a group of syilx smǝlqmíx Youth “fighting for the water,” hosted an event on Sunday in the town of Keremeos, speaking about

their “refusal”

 of the Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle expansion.


More than 50 people of all ages and backgrounds were in attendance, with many displaying signs with messages that read “No to the Ingerbelle Mine Expansion.” 


After years of deliberating,

the “B.C.” government greenlit the New Ingerbelle expansion in February

, issuing Mines Act and Environmental Management Act permits. The open pit gold and copper mine is located near “Princeton” in smǝlqmíx territory, which is about an hour northwest of Keremeos.


There have been years-long concerns from syilx communities and advocates about the impact that the expansion of the mine and its already towering tailings dam will have on the Similkameen River,

which some worry

 could have “catastrophic impacts” on the valley. 


The expansion will see the mine’s existing 192-metre tailings dam — roughly equivalent in height to a 58-storey building — increased by an additional 87 metres,

according to the province’s Environmental Assessment Office (EAO)

.


While acknowledging that she was “angry” and “upset” to have to stand up for the water; the land; and all the beings that rely on them, nmlqitkʷ defender Meadow Arcand said on Sunday that the Indigenous Youth “have a responsibility to do this work.”


“What we’re really looking out for is these young ones, the sacred ones that are going to come after us. Like our ancestors did before us, like our Elders did before us, like the old people did before us,” said Arcand.


“We’re standing here so people can’t say that we didn’t.”


She extended this same responsibility to anyone benefitting from Okanagan waters and territories – not just syilx smǝlqmíx people.


“We need people to care about our relationships with all life: with the water, with each other, and with the future generations,” she said.


“What we do here now matters. What our ancestors did matters.”


More than 50 people gathered in Keremeos on Nov. 8 to stand in solidarity with nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders, a group of syilx smǝlqmíx Youth who are opposed to the nearby Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle Expansion project.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’


Older generations of the smǝlqmíx community also spoke on Sunday, denouncing the mine expansion and sharing their support for the Youth. The organizers left handouts to resources – such as their online

petition

 and

declaration

 – and other information bulletins on what’s happening with mining in their homelands.


They also brought with them the syilx Okanagan Nation’s

siwɬkʷ (Water) Declaration

.


The expansion project is set to see the century-old mining operation revive its old Ingerbelle open pit gold and copper mine site near the Similkameen River. The expansion will extend the mining’s operation until 2047, according to the province.


After the province greenlit the mine’s expansion project in February, leadership at both Upper and Lower Similkameen Indian Bands (USIB, LSIB)

denounced the government’s decision

, saying that “no consent” was given.


y̓ilmixʷm (Chief) kalʔlùpaɋʹn Keith Crow of LSIB told IndigiNews in 2022 that the Similkameen River is the lifeblood of the valley.


“If we lose that, we lose our identity. We lose who we are,” Crow said.


An aerial view of the Similkameen River, flowing through the town of Keremeos in smǝlqmíx homelands in December 2024.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Meanwhile, the mine’s owner Hudbay Minerals

issued a statement

 saying it “proactively engaged” with USIB and LSIB throughout the permitting process, and “finalized refreshed participation agreements” with both communities — “reinforcing the company’s commitment to …

title: C4SS Panelists on the Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie
content:
There will be a Molinari/C4SS presence at the 10th annual PPE Society meeting, 12-14 November 2026, at the Westin New Orleans (100 Iberville St.).


I’ve organised a panel on “The Intellectual Legacy of Don Lavoie.” We’re in the very first session of the conference: Thursday, 12 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in River Room II.


The panel features Cory Massimino (C4SS) on “National Economic Planning: What is Right?” and Nathan Goodman (Mercatus; co-authoring with Molly Rovinski and Karla Segovia) on “Immigration Restrictions as Non-Comprehensive Planning.” Zak Woodman was also scheduled to speak at the panel, on “Ratcheting Up State Power: The Knowledge Problem, the Power Problem, and Legibility,” but will probably not be able to make it.


(This is not to be confused with the panel on the same topic at last month’s Mercatus Markets & Society conference, organised by Nathan Goodman and featuring Jason Byas, Akiva Malamet, and again Cory Massimino.)


Jason Byas, currently in his first year as Assistant Professor in Philosophy and Political Economy at Tulane, is also on the program; he’ll be speaking in a panel on “Anarchism as a Practical Philosophy,” Friday, 13 November 2026, 9:00-10:30 a.m. (Central time) in the Salon Room. Jason’s fellow panelists are Jesse Spafford, Jessica Flanigan, and Billy Christmas.

author: Valerie Anne
title: You Oughta Know That Alanis Morissette Is Pansexual
content:
feature image photo by Credit: NBC / Contributor via Getty Images

It’s official: 90s icon and present-day superstar Alanis Morissette is pansexual. The singer was a guest on the Handsome podcast, which is co-hosted by queer comedians Tig Notaro, Fortune Feimster, and Mae Martin, and they were talking about Alanis’s penchant for a post-breakup rage anthem. Fortune Feimster jokingly asked her, “Did it make you want to be a lesbian at any point?” to which Alanis replied, “I’m pansexual, so yeah.”

The energy in the room was perfect. At first, everyone thought it was a joke (or perhaps that she was being…ironic), but when they clarified that Alanis was serious, they all joked that she should have led with that. You walk into a queer podcast with the queer announcement!!

Granted, this is not the first time Alanis has said she isn’t straight. She has been talking about exploring her sexuality and being attracted to women as far back as 2008, and it was apparently at least partly her idea for her character to kiss Sarah Jessica Parker’s Carrie during her Sex and the City guest spot. It’s just the first time she’s used a specific label out loud.

I considered riddling this intro with Alanis-related puns (like the joke my friend made: she’s got one pan in her pocket…) but I’ll save you the cringe. I’ll just say this news has made me even more head over feet for her.

God is a woman, and she’s also pansexual.

You Live, You Learn (About More Gay News)

Cara Delevingne sent Reneé Rapp for a loop during a prank call in an Elle interview.

Speaking of Cara Delevingne, she also was at the red carpet premiere of Club Kid talking about the movie and also the “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections.

Beanie Feldstein and her wife welcomed a baby girl into their family (Beanie already made the “beanie baby” joke so I will refrain).

Amber Glenn took the lead in her Dancing with the Stars number on Disney night, dressed in shiny white pants, flexing her impressive-as-hell back muscles, and doing the quickstep to A Star is Born from Hercules.

Queer Swedish pop star Tove Styrke returns to music after having a baby with her partner Sanna Sikborn Erixon.

Cynthia Nixon was asked who her favorite lesbian is and she said Sappho (and also gave almost-definitely-bisexual Eleanor Roosevelt a shout-out).

The wait is almost over: Netflix’s The Body drops on Wednesday, November 11.

Queer Canadian icon Jann Arden is among the recognizable names on the guest star list for Jared Keeso’s upcoming comedy I Kill the Bear, alongside other queer-adjacent faves like Melanie Scrofano, Michelle Mylett, and Tricia Helfer.

ICYMI, WNBA players Azzi Fudd and Paige Bueckers have actually been broken up for quite a while, but don’t worry, they’re still friends.

author: Victoria Valenzuela
title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.


Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.


“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”


Los Padrinos had

reopened a year earlier

 in 2023, after being shut down in 2019 due to conditions that violated the Board of State and Community Corrections (BSCC) standards, including abuses by staff. Six officers were criminally charged with

assault and child abuse

 for using pepper spray on several teenage girls. Reports

also cited a decreasing youth population

 as a factor for closure, yet staff

claimed to feel “outnumbered.”

 When Los Padrinos closed, youth were shuffled to another facility called Central Juvenile Hall — and then in 2023, that facility was closed down due to similar issues. Los Padrinos reopened, and just months later, the abuses restarted. In 2025,

30 officers were criminally charged

 by the California Attorney General with child endangerment and abuse, conspiracy, and battery for encouraging “gladiator fights” that pit youth against each other.


Olivia Shields, a justice transformation policy coordinator at Urban Peace Institute, described the constant closing and reopening of BSCC facilities as a “cycle of noncompliance.” Shields said the Los Angeles County Probation Department has ultimately failed with these maneuvers to address the core issue: unmet youth needs — which won’t be addressed through incarceration but through coordinated care in the form of individualized, robust support systems and resources.


“Rather than decarcerate these populations of young people and find community-based alternatives or step-downs for as many of them as possible, they basically shift the youth around from facility to facility to avoid noncompliance,” Shields said.


Long before the closing of Los Padrinos in 2019, the facility had a bad reputation among Angelenos. Maradiaga recalled hearing disturbing stories about the facility in the ’80s when she was a kid.


“I think it needs to be shut down,” Maradiaga said. “I think that there needs to be a better way for the youth. I don’t think locking them away from their family is the answer.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Barred From Basic Human Contact


When Ilana Parach, executive director and co-founder of

Hoops 4 Justice

, went inside Los Padrinos with a basketball and mentorship program, she quickly learned about what youth were facing inside. She felt it was important to give them a platform to express their needs directly, so she pivoted to working with them on legislation.


“They made a list of specific programs they wanted — resources for their families, reentry support,” Parach said. “At the bottom of that list, they wrote, ‘We want to hug our moms.’”


Incarcerated youth directly told her that one parent who hugged her son during a visit on his birthday then had her visit terminated and future visits suspended for two weeks. She said another youth was incarcerated for three years and had no choice but to watch his mother cry during the visits because she couldn’t hug him.


Contact visitation policies vary across California and are often left at the discretion of correctional officers. Parach said youth and staff both told her that Los Padrinos stopped allowing contact visits after the pandemic. Parach said that during meetings of the board of supervisors, she heard officers citing staffing shortages …

title: In the Crosshairs of the Far-Right Advance : An Update on Anti-Fascists and Anarchists in Greece
content:
Anarchist graffiti from Athens, Greece (2026)


The anarchist movement in Greece faces a new wave of repression. Urged on by the US and its obsession with combatting “far-left extremism,” the Greek state has targeted anti-authoritarians with new legal charges and attacked demonstrations, while fascists carry out street attacks and plot their return to the halls of power. Amidst a landscape of ongoing austerity, terrorism designations, lethal prisons, and ferocious wildfires, anarchists nonetheless continue to forge a combative culture of revolutionary solidarity.


In this article, we present an interview with an anarchist comrade in Athens assessing the current situation among anarchists and anti-fascists in Greece, along with analysis of the US’s role in advancing state repression and fantasies of Western supremacy.


The US and Greece: A Right-Wing Alliance to Defend “The West”


Earlier this month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a speech at the Pnyx in Athens. With the historic Acropolis and the Parthenon—that ancient symbol of Western democracy, constructed with slave labor—in the background, he delivered a warning message to Greece’s political and business elite.


“The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” Rubio cautioned. “We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.” Lamenting how “nationalism became a dirty word,” he called for renewed militarism, praised Christian faith and martyrdom, and announced a new counterterrorism information-sharing program between the two countries. His statements were calculated to reinforce the colonial legacy of Western dominance over the rest of the world, while urging the worst of Greek society to imitate America’s current political trajectory.


US Secretary of State Marco Rubio constructs an elaborate photo op for his defense of nationalism, militarism, and “the West” (October 7, 2026).


The speech came in the wake of a conference Rubio convened in July that aimed to coordinate intensified repression against “far-left extremism.” The following month, the US government imposed a “global terrorist” designation on the Italy-based

Autistici/Inventati (A/I) tech collective

, which operated the free publishing platform NoBlogs.org.


Greece’s right-wing politicians and business leaders benefiting from the country’s endless austerity measures are heeding Rubio’s call to preserve the hubris of the so-called West. Meanwhile, governments are collaborating to escalate repression against any truly revolutionary movements that challenge the world’s current status quo.


Greece’s strategic importance to Western powers is rooted in its symbolic status as the birthplace of “Western Civilization,” as well as its strategic location in the world today. The country offers the US access to four military sites, including a dedicated Navy base in Crete’s Souda Bay. Those with a longer memory have not forgotten how the US supplied napalm to Greece’s fascist forces, who worked with the Nazis during World War II and later with the British and US in a Cold War anti-communist alliance. Fascists dropped American napalm on Greek partisan resistance fighters during the civil war from 1946 to 1949, scorching bodies and charring forests, leaving the countryside scarred to this day.


More recently, the Greek people were pummeled by the 2008 global economic crisis, brought on in part by Wall Street firms such as Goldman Sachs that raked in immense profits while destabilizing the world’s economy and immiserating millions. The US then contributed to the austerity measures imposed on Greece in 2010 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), leading to years of ferocious resistance to neoliberal capitalism and government complicity.


Today, Greece’s current New Democracy regime upholds

the legacy of the brutal military junta

 of 1967-1974, promoting the image of Greece as a symbol European supremacy as invoked by Rubio. Despite its nationalist rhetoric, the government continues to lick the boots of the US, crushing opposition in the streets and enforcing a never-ending precarity on the majority of Greece’s increasingly exhausted and numb population.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Otra muerte por asbesto en el subte: anuncian medidas de fuerza
content:
La Asociación Gremial de Trabajadores del Subterráneo y Premetro (AGTSYP – Metrodelegadxs) informó una nueva muerte causada por la exposición al asbesto, un cancerígeno mortal. Ya son 7 los trabajadores fallecidos y 130 afectados por esta causa.


En 2011, Mauricio Macri –entonces jefe de Gobierno de la Ciudad– adquirió sin licitación previa al Metro de Madrid 36 vagones que se encontraban fuera de circulación en España.


A principios del 2017, los trabajadores españoles avisaron a los Metrodelegados que los subtes que se habían vendido a la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, que Macri y Rodríguez Larreta habían ido a comprar, estaban atestados de asbesto. Esos mismos coches eran los que había estado enfermando a los trabajadores del Metro de Madrid con las afecciones que empezaron a afectar a las y los trabajadores argentinos del Subte. También las y los pasajeros están en riesgo.


Entonces comenzó la lucha de los trabajadores de la AGTSyP por la eliminación de este mineral cancerígeno, que en la Argentina está prohibido desde 2003.


Uno de los invitados al VIP fue el empresario Aldo Roggio.


Es el dueño del Subte.


Está semana se murió el 7mo trabajador del subte por exposición al asbesto, un material cancerígeno.


Se había jubilado y le dejaron de cubrir los estudios.


— ari lijalad (@arilijalad)

November 11, 2026


El sindicato señala que el asbesto está presente en toda la red del subte porteño, no sólo en los trenes sino también en instalaciones, transformadores, tendidos eléctricos, infraestructura edilicia.


Compartimos el comunicado:


OTRA MUERTE POR ASBESTO EN EL SUBTE


MEDIDAS DE AUTODEFENSA


Desde la Asociación Gremial de Trabajadores del Subterráneo y Premetro (AGTSYP – Metrodelegadxs) lamentamos anunciar el fallecimiento de un compañero jubilado que trabajó durante 30 años expuesto al asbesto, por lo que el servicio se encontrará interrumpido el día jueves 12 de noviembre, desde las 21hs hasta el cierre.


El compañero trabajó en los talleres Polvorín / Bonifacio y en el Taller Rancagua, uno de los lugares con mayor exposición al asbesto de toda la red.


Los trabajadores expuestos al asbesto tienen controles médicos periódicos, pero estos controles cesan al momento de jubilarse. Nuestro sindicato viene reclamando hace años que los jubilados continúen en vigilancia médica, para detectar a tiempo las enfermedades derivadas de esta contaminación y poder evitar muertes como la de nuestro compañero.


La afección por exposición al asbesto tiene una latencia de 40 años, lo que implica que décadas después de haber trabajado en el Subte y Premetro, pueden despertarse enfermedades relacionadas a la exposición.


En el subte hay 7 trabajadores fallecidos y 130 afectados por la exposición al asbesto. No podemos seguir lamentando muertes que son evitables, nadie tendría que morir por su trabajo.


Todas las personas que trabajan en el Subte y Premetro deben ser incorporadas a Vigilancia Médica, que debe extenderse también a las y los trabajadores jubilados. Seguimos exigiendo un subte y premetro libre de asbesto.


La entrada

Otra muerte por asbesto en el subte: anuncian medidas de fuerza

 se publicó primero en

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Protestos de jovens pelo mundo demonstram que ainda se pode sonhar com o futuro
content:
Uma onda de protestos liderados pela Geração Z está se levantando pelo mundo, trazendo uma lufada de ar fresco e remodelando cenários políticos. 


Nós vimos isso

no Brasil com os atos encabeçados por movimentos estudantis que puxaram milhares de pessoas para as ruas e atuaram fortemente nas redes pela democracia e pela reeleição de Lula.


Na Itália, as jornadas estudantis pedem mais verbas para a educação pública

, melhorias em infraestrutura escolar e medidas contra o altíssimo custo de aluguéis e moradias estudantis.

Na França, protestos que começaram em setembro também por demandas de melhor educação, melhor infraestrutura nas escolas e mais investimento, têm se intensificado e tomado as ruas de todo o país

 –  só no último dia 05, reuniram cerca de 600 mil pessoas, segundo números oficiais.

Na Alemanha, o movimento Gen Z Regelt (Algo como “A Geração Z Resolve”) realizou atos em 34 cidades para protestar contra o serviço militar obrigatório e exigir mais investimentos em educação

, e no dia 31 de outubro botou nas ruas cerca de 120 mil pessoas.


Na Índia, o movimento Partido do Povo Barata (CJP, na sigla em inglês para


Cockroach Janta Party

) também tem levado milhares de jovens às ruas de Mumbai e Nova Deli para denunciar irregularidades na educação

, pedir a saída do ministro da Educação, Dharmendra Pradhan, e uma reforma no sistema de exames. O CJP é um movimento político liderado pela Geração Z indiana que surgiu a partir de declarações feitas em maio pelo presidente do Supremo Tribunal da Índia, que usou o termo “barata” para descrever jovens desempregados que se dedicam ao ativismo.


Os protestos movidos pelos GenZ – nascidos entre 1997 e 2012 – geralmente levantam pautas relacionadas à educação, mas também pedem a cabeça de líderes autoritários, atenção à emergência climática, às desigualdades sociais e abordam conflitos como o Genocídio em Gaza. São campanhas horizontais, sem um líder específico, e que usam as redes sociais para se organizar.


A repressão também tem sido violenta. Não é possível dizer o número certo de prisões porque os atos seguem acontecendo, mas estima-se que mais de 6 mil pessoas foram presas somente na França, sendo 87% delas menores de idade.


Em uma

análise recente, a Civicus,

 organização sem fins lucrativos que monitora as liberdades civis globais, afirmou:

“Como questionam a distribuição do poder econômico e político, os protestos liderados pela geração Z invariavelmente são recebidos com violência estatal”.

 O relatório relaciona a violência infligida aos jovens manifestantes com seu foco em sistemas e instituições que há muito tempo estavam simplesmente sendo aceitos.


Protestos liderados por movimentos estudantis não são novidade, claro. Mas o que torna essa nova onda interessante é o momento em que ela se levanta. 


Em um mundo que tem sido assolado por governos autoritários e populistas que fazem conchavos com Big Techs para intermediar todas as relações humanas e interferir na soberania de países, que incentivam o ódio, a misoginia, criam e alimentam um ambiente tóxico e violento para mulheres e LGBTQIA+, em um momento de múltiplas instabilidades, guerras e crises – climáticas, econômicas, institucionais, crises que desafiam o que entendemos por democracia e como víamos a política institucional e crises que atingem em cheio o modelo capitalista neoliberal que nos engole com seu ultra individualismo –

os jovens vêm cobrar o que nunca lhes foi prometido. Eles vêm dizer que querem eles mesmos criar futuro. 


Pode parecer óbvio, mas não é.


Porque a essa geração foi oferecido pouco espaço para utopia, pouca imaginação de futuro, pouco encantamento.

 Para usar o termo que Paolo Demuru cunha em seu livro “Políticas do Encanto”: pouca perspectiva. Afinal, vivemos muitos pontos de não retorno. 


Ao mesmo tempo, o futuro baseado em um passado fantasioso prometido pela extrema direita, em que a emergência climática é mentira, que diz que é só expulsar imigrante que o emprego vem e a economia melhora, ou, na sua versão tecno-solucionista, que a IA resolveria todos os males do planeta, simplesmente não está acontecendo.


É nesse vácuo que

a Geração Z ocupa as ruas, recusa tanto o passado inventado da extrema direita quanto o futuro tecno-solucionista das Big Techs, e reivindica o direito de imaginar. 


Bonito ver esses jovens devolverem à política algo que parecia perdido: a ideia de que o futuro ainda está em disputa e que dá para construí-lo …

author: anred
title: «La identidad no necesita cura»: reclaman al Papa León XIV y a la Iglesia acompañar a sobrevivientes de las terapias de conversión
content:
Foto: David Silverman//Getty Images


En el marco de la visita del Papa León XIV en la Argentina, la organización argentina de Gualeguaychú «Nada que curar» envió una carta al arzobispo metropolitano de Buenos Aires, Jorge Ignacio García Cuerva, para solicitar el acompañamiento de la Iglesia Católica a su trabajo con personas LGBTIQ+ que sobrevivieron a prácticas de conversión. La iniciativa, cofundada por Pablo Ignacio Echeverría, desarrolla espacios de escucha entre pares y recursos educativos para quienes atraviesan procesos de reconstrucción de sus creencias religiosas sobre sexualidad y género. La presentación se conoció en la semana de la visita del papa León XIV a la Argentina y vuelve a poner en discusión el papel de las instituciones religiosas en prácticas que buscan modificar o reprimir orientaciones sexuales e identidades de género. «Nuestra iniciativa parte de la premisa de que la identidad no necesita cura», señala la carta, que propone abrir un espacio de diálogo pastoral para escuchar a sobrevivientes, reparar heridas producidas en contextos de fe y construir caminos para vivir la espiritualidad y la identidad en libertad.

Por ANRed.


La organización argentina de Gualeguaychú «

Nada que curar»

 envió una carta al arzobispo metropolitano de Buenos Aires,

Jorge Ignacio García Cuerva

, para solicitar el

acompañamiento de la Iglesia Católica a su trabajo con personas LGBTIQ+ que atravesaron prácticas de conversión

. La presentación, fechada el 6 de noviembre y difundida por el medio local

R2820

, se conoció en plena semana de la

visita del Papa León XIV a la Argentina

. La iniciativa, cofundada por el gualeguaychuense

Pablo Ignacio Echeverría

 —conocido como «Pholo»—, trabaja en la intersección entre

diversidad sexual y espiritualidad

, con especial atención a

quienes sufrieron intentos de modificar o reprimir su orientación sexual o identidad de género

.


En la carta, la organización se presenta como «un proyecto argentino de acompañamiento entre pares destinado a personas LGBTIQ+ que atraviesan procesos de deconstrucción de creencias religiosas sobre sexualidad y género, con especial énfasis en sobrevivientes de prácticas de conversión (ECOSIG/ECOSIEG)». Y afirma: «

nuestra iniciativa parte de la premisa de que la identidad no necesita cura y busca ayudar a encontrar paz a aquellas personas que, dentro de contextos religiosos, han visto tratada su sexualidad como una enfermedad que debe ser sanada»

. El equipo está integrado por profesionales, sobrevivientes y activistas de Santa Fe, Gualeguaychú, Córdoba y Buenos Aires, y aclara que su tarea no consiste en brindar tratamiento clínico, sino en ofrecer escucha y acompañamiento comunitario.


Imagen: Prensa ATE


Uno de los puntos centrales del documento es que

estas prácticas no siempre aparecen bajo el nombre de «terapias de conversión»

. Según advierten,

continúan desarrollándose en ámbitos religiosos y familiares mediante propuestas presentadas como «sanidad interior», «liberación», «restauración» o incluso «Terapias psicológicas individuales y de acompañamiento familiar»

. En esa línea, la organización sostiene que muchas personas que se acercan a sus espacios no habían logrado identificar como prácticas de conversión las situaciones que habían vivido: «la mayoría de las personas que se acercan a nosotros nunca habían logrado identificar lo que vivieron como una ‘terapia de conversión’ hasta dar con ese nombre», advierten.


El problema también aparece documentado en el

primer informe federal sobre prácticas de conversión en Argentina, elaborado por la Asociación de Familias Diversas de Argentina (AFDA)

 con apoyo de Outright International y publicado en 2025. La investigación reunió respuestas de 839 personas LGBTI+ y entrevistas a 20 sobrevivientes y nueve actores relevantes. Entre las personas sobrevivientes encuestadas,

el 57,5% señaló a líderes religiosos como promotores de estas prácticas y el 51,67% mencionó a familiares

. En cuanto a sus consecuencias, se registraron

sentimientos de culpa, ansiedad, baja autoestima, vergüenza, depresión y aislamiento; un 45,92% reportó ideación suicida

. Se trata de porcentajes corresponden a quienes respondieron el relevamiento y no constituyen una estimación de la población LGBTI+ del país.


Foto: David McNew//Getty Images


En Argentina existe un marco normativo que protege indirectamente a las personas frente a estas prácticas, aunque no una ley nacional específica que las …

author: Rizomatica
title: Sobre la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley indigena 19.253
content:
La propuesta de modificación al artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 impulsada en el gobierno anterior a través de la denominada Comisión para la Paz y Entendimiento, fue una iniciativa transversal de la clase Política que incluyó a personeros de todo el espectro político Chileno como propuesta para el desarrollo en materia indígena.


Está propuesta ha sido fomentada por el actual gobierno de tinte ultraderechista con la finalidad de instalarla cómo política pública para el pueblo mapuche. Prueba de ello es que hace pocos días se reunieron en Temuco diversos personeros del gobierno con la finalidad de promover una consulta para dar implementación a esta medida.


El artículo 13 de la ley 19.253 es la normativa que regula y contiene restricciones respecto del dominio y uso de los terrenos indígenas. Este artículo contiene una protección exigida por el interés nacional del cual son sujetos los terrenos indígenas que impide que estos sean sometidos a enajenaciones, embargos, gravámenes, ni ser adquiridas por prescripción, salvo entre comunidades o personas de una misma etnia.


En términos generales, hasta ahora, el artículo 13 ha sido una salvaguarda para el dominio de la tierra indígena en manos de los pueblos originarios, por cuánto la ley en este aspecto tiene un carácter imperativo y obligatorio de protección.


No obstante aquello, esto no ha significado una protección completa ya que a través de diversos artilugios legales se han registrado casos en que a pesar de sus diversas prohibiciones, si se ha logrado enajenar (

vender

) terrenos indígenas a personas no mapuche. Esto ha sido en virtud de vacíos contenidos en la normativa que dejan espacios a artilugios legales que diversos abogados han utilizado para realizar esas ventas en vulneración al espíritu de la ley.


Un caso emblemático a este respecto fue el mediático caso de la venta realizada por la viuda chilena de un mapuche después de su muerte en la comuna de Pucón al ex subsecretario Ubilla durante el gobierno del expresidente Piñera.


Está venta de un terreno indígena a un chileno dejó de manifiesto lo frágil de la ley respecto de la real protección a los terrenos indígenas cuando hay intereses económicos importantes de por medio. Esta venta se pudo realizar en el contexto de lo que en derecho civil se conoce como liquidación de una sociedad conyugal y adjudicación por disolución de esta.


Volviendo a la propuesta de modificación al artículo 13, lo que preocupa es el aparente sentido inocuo de dicha medida, ya que directamente no habla de

enajenación

 o

venta

 de un terreno indígena a una persona o entidad no mapuche, sino que el énfasis ha sido puesto en la posibilidad de

arrendamiento

 de un terreno indígena a personas

no indígenas

 o

personas


jurídicas

 de diversa índole.


Está situación es más compleja de lo que parece a simple vista porque abre una posibilidad de vulneraciones difíciles de prever a futuro.


Lo que señala la propuesta de modificación es que los terrenos indígenas podrán ser arrendados a cualquier persona no indígena o persona jurídica por un plazo de hasta 10 años y 25 años con consulta al órgano técnico encargado en materia indígena que es la Conadi.


El argumento para esto, es que en las condiciones actuales de restricción que contiene la propiedad indígena ha sido muy difícil incorporar estos terrenos a los beneficios que contempla la ley y a diversas medidas administrativas de los órganos y servicios del Estado en materia de fomento productivo, acceso a vivienda, acceso a crédito, transferencia tecnológica y oportunidades de desarrollo en general. En la visión de los promotores de esta iniciativa se sostiene que esto ha sido el principal elemento de tope que han tenido los mapuche para hacer productivas sus tierras e incorporarlas eficientemente al circuito productivo de la economía local y regional.


Para ello se propone bajar el nivel de restricciones que contiene la ley en materia de protección y permitir arriendos en condiciones de mercado actuales y competitivos.


Esto en teoría significaría regular de forma más eficiente situaciones de arriendo irregular que hoy pudiesen existir y por otra parte mejorar los promedios de los valores de los precios de arriendo para el arrendador y conceder garantías tanto de tiempo como de condiciones jurídicas que permitan al arrendatario realizar una labor productiva con seguridad en un tiempo acorde a dicha inversión, pudiendo ser por un lapso de hasta 25 años.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Día de la Maestra y el Maestro Rural: sembrar el derecho a la educación en cerros, llanuras y bosques
content:
Por Marcela Isaías


El primer día de su trabajo Leila quedó largas horas empantanada en el camino hacia la escuela. Ese fue su bautismo como maestra rural en el norte santafesino. Sandra enseña arte en secundarias rurales de Entre Ríos; todo el tiempo denuncia el mal estado de las rutas y la fumigación de los campos con agrotóxicos. El femicidio de la directora correntina Nancy Godoy le llegó muy de cerca. Adolfo da clases en un pueblo jujeño cercano a La Quiaca, en sus tareas diarias incluye la huerta escolar como un espacio de encuentro con las familias.


Ni heroínas ni apóstoles. Historias que hablan de cómo trabajan maestras y maestros rurales para garantizar el derecho a la educación.


Norte de Santa Fe


Leila Díaz vive en Tostado, cabecera del departamento 9 de Julio, bien al norte de la provincia de Santa Fe. Desde el año pasado es maestra reemplazante, siempre en la ruralidad. Su primera suplencia la hizo en una escuela rural ubicada a unos 44 kilómetros de Tostado. Una buena parte del trayecto hasta ese establecimiento es por un camino de tierra, y sí o sí lo tiene que hacer en un vehículo propio. “La primera vez que fui me llevó mi papá. Hacía dos días había llovido y en el primer charco nos quedamos”, repasa ese recuerdo que atesora.


Con ella viajaba la cocinera de la escuela. Llevaban las provisiones de comida para la semana, la garrafa, agua, además de los materiales y útiles para las clases. Debieron caminar varios kilómetros hasta el cruce con la ruta para buscar ayuda.


Leila había soñado con ese primer día de trabajo como maestra, “nunca con algo parecido” a lo que pasó. Igual siguió adelante y se enamoró de la enseñanza rural: “Lo maravilloso fue cuando llegamos a la escuela, conectamos el wi-fiy mandé un mensaje al grupo de las familias para que sepan que iba a haber clases. A los dos o tres minutos empezaron a llegar todos los niños y las niñas. Ahí entendí lo importantes que somos”.


Foto: Gentileza Leila Díaz


Vivir la semana en el lugar donde enseña es parte de su trabajo. Por lo general, quienes permanecen en estas experiencias son la docente, que hace también tareas de dirección al ser personal único, la portera o cocinera y la maestra de nivel inicial. “Las tres solitas en el medio de la nada”, dice recordando una noche de tormenta en la que además se cortó la luz.


Leila se explaya en la charla sobre su vida familiar, su hija pequeña, su marido. Del intercambio que tiene con sus alumnas y alumnos, que enriquecen la experiencia pedagógica y remiten al legado freiriano: “Siento que me escuchan, que se llevan algo de mí, como yo me llevo de ellos, porque siempre me están enseñando”.


En ese ir y venir de relatos, reconoce que no puede dejar de pensar en lo que le pasó a Nancy Godoy, la docente correntina víctima de un atroz femicidio. “Pude haber sido yo o cualquiera de mis compañeras. Todas nos sentimos identificadas con ella”, comenta ese sentimiento de espanto colectivo.


“Después de lo que pasó con Nancy —continúa— te preguntás hasta qué punto te podés exponer. Más cuando, en Santa Fe, un reemplazo lo cobrás a los 60 días”.


Las condiciones laborales, en particular la movilidad, se vuelve un tema ineludible, atraviesa todo el tiempo la conversación con quienes ejercen en la ruralidad. Si hay que hacer dedo “siempre tratamos de ser dos o más, ir en grupo”. Pide más empatía a quienes tienen a su cargo las escuelas y exigen llegar sí o sí a dar clases, “sin importar a costa de qué”.


Cierta vez viajaba en auto junto a otras maestras a dar clases a la localidad de Esteban Rams, a 77 kilómetros de Tostado. Por la imprudencia de otro conductor estuvieron a poco de un accidente: “Nos salvamos de milagro”. Es ineludible la mención a la tragedia del 27 de mayo de 2013, ocurrida en el norte santafesino y en la que perdieron la vida diez personas, entre ellas siete maestras. Pasaron más de diez años y el reclamo para que se atienda el traslado cuidadoso de la docencia rural sigue pendiente.


Daniela Spárvoli fue víctima de femicidio en 2003 - Foto: Amsafe Delegación Iriondo


Nancy y Daniela


El femicidio de Nancy Godoy puso en la agenda pública otra vez el trabajo de las docentes rurales. Nancy era de Esquina (Corrientes) y desde agosto pasado ejercía como directora suplente en la Escuela Rural N° 626, en el Paraje El Malezal. author: La Zarzamora
title: Lanzamiento de Black Onions, un listado de sitios web anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion
content:
Publicado originalmente en Montréal Contre-information

Nos complace anunciar el lanzamiento de Black Onions, una nueva iniciativa que tiene como objetivo ofrecer una lista estable y actualizada periódicamente de sitios anarquistas y antiautoritarios con extensión .onion. Los sitios .onion son sitios web accesibles a través del navegador Tor mediante direcciones que terminan en «.onion».

En los últimos meses, algunos gobiernos han atacado las infraestructuras de comunicación de nuestros movimientos con renovado vigor; buena prueba de ello son la conferencia internacional sobre el «terrorismo de extrema izquierda» celebrada en Estados Unidos en julio, así como la inclusión del proveedor de servicios de alojamiento militante italiano Autistici/Inventati en una lista de sanciones relacionadas con el terrorismo a finales de agosto.

Para bien o para mal, la comunicación pública de nuestros movimientos tiene lugar en gran medida en Internet, lo que la hace vulnerable a los mecanismos tecnológicos de censura. A diferencia de los sitios web convencionales, los sitios .onion son menos vulnerables a la censura, ya que no utilizan nombres de dominio y permiten ocultar la ubicación del servidor, del mismo modo que el navegador Tor oculta tu propia ubicación al visitar el sitio. Consideramos que los sitios .onion son nuestra mejor baza para seguir comunicándonos en línea dentro del movimiento anarquista, especialmente si los intentos de censura se intensifican en el futuro.

El problema recurrente de los sitios .onion es que sus direcciones, compuestas por 56 caracteres aleatorios, son imposibles de memorizar. Black Onions tiene como objetivo resolver este problema. Te recomendamos guardar en los marcadores del navegador Tor, o en un archivo en tu ordenador, las direcciones .onion que utilizas habitualmente; pero si necesitas una dirección que aún no has guardado, ¡encuéntrala en Black Onions!

Accede a Black Onions a través de cualquiera de las siguientes direcciones:

– blackonions.gd – blackonions.li – blackonions.st – (próximamente, una dirección .onion)

Para establecer una base de confianza en esta nueva iniciativa, los siguientes proyectos anarquistas han avalado nuestra propuesta mediante declaraciones firmadas con PGP: Act For Freedom Now!, un proyecto de contrainformación activo desde 2008 , y el No Trace Project, un proyecto contra la represión activo desde 2021.

¡Utiliza sitios .onion! ¡Resiste a la censura!

author: CMI Argentina
title: Exigen reconocimiento de enfermedades laborales en escuelas por agrotóxicos
content:
Más de 165 organizaciones sindicales y colectivos socioambientales presentaron un petitorio ante la Dirección General de Cultura y Educación bonaerense (DGCyE), en La Plata, con más de 3.000 firmas de integrantes de comunidades educativas y de la población en general, para exigirle al Estado el reconocimiento de las enfermedades laborales de trabajadores/as de la educación originadas por la exposición a las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos y al consumo de agua con estos elementos, y por el efecto sinérgico que se produce por su combinación con agua contaminada con niveles de arsénico más elevados de lo permitido por normativa, en las instituciones educativas.


“Los casos de las compañeras maestras Ana Zabaloy en San Antonio de Areco (pcia Bs As), víctima de asesinato laboral por trabajar en condiciones insalubres en una escuela rural y a quien el Estado nunca le reconoció su enfermedad oncológica en el marco de la Ley de Riesgos de Trabajo; y de Estela Lemes en Entre Ríos, quien presenta agrotóxicos en sangre y tuvo que judicializar su situación para que le reconozcan su enfermedad laboral, son ejemplos contundentes del impacto del agronegocio en la salud. Se suman argumentos a nuestro planteo con la reciente investigación y denuncia protagonizada por el sindicato AMSAFE Rosario del 2024 (en ese entonces con la conducción de la Lista Multicolor) que demostró que docentes y auxiliares de distintas escuelas presentaban daño génico por la presencia de agrotóxicos en su ambiente laboral”, detallan las organizaciones, al tiempo que invitan a Sindicatos Docentes y de Auxiliares de la Educación a que se sumen a esta demanda.


Entre las medidas urgentes que reclaman las organizaciones se encuentran el reconocimiento inmediato, y con carácter retroactivo, de las enfermedades laborales productos del agronegocio; la implementación de programas permanentes de vigilancia sanitaria para docentes y auxiliares; la realización de análisis integrales del agua en todos los establecimientos educativos, donde se provea agua segura hasta tanto se demuestre su potabilidad; medidas de protección con aumento de distancias progresivas ante las fumigaciones de agrotóxicos para garantizar las condiciones mínimas de seguridad e higiene en cada escuela, en función de que se cumplan los derechos laborales básicos.


“La salud de las comunidades educativas no puede esperar. Exigimos respuestas concretas y medidas urgentes para garantizar el derecho a la salud y a condiciones de trabajo y de enseñanza seguras”, reclaman las organizaciones.

title: Serokê Nivîsîngehê pêşwaziyê li Konsulê Giştî yê Tirkiyeyê kir
content:
Nîvroya îro Çarşem 11/11/2026, birêz Dr. Nûrî Osman, Serokê Nivîsîngeha Serokê Herêma Kurdistanê, pêşwaziyê li birêz Erman Topçu, Konsulê Giştî yê Tirkiyeyê li Herêma Kurdistanê kir. Di hevdîtinê de, peywendiyên Iraq û Herêma Kurdistanê bi Tirkiyeyê re û awayê pêşxistina wan gûftûgo kirin.
