author: rti_admin
title: A Ballot and the Barricade
content:
Quite often, as I stand at the edge of Jantar Mantar and watch a police officer tighten the barricades across the road, I see space. It surprises me, for, like democracy or citizenship or the human right to protest, space is not supposed to be seen. It is not that standing in New Delhi, this capital of monumental avenues, government buildings and carefully cultivated national spectacles, has given me some special ability to see what I had not been able to see before. It is just that, when the police begin deciding where people can stand, how far they can walk and how long they can remain together, space suddenly acquires a very visible grammar. Everything competes with it for visibility: placards, police uniforms, detention vans, commuters searching for an alternative route, journalists trying to document an unfolding confrontation and, of course, the institutions that seem much easier to approach in a textbook than on the street. Light, which can illuminate a public institution, cannot necessarily illuminate the distance between that institution and the people who wish to question it. On 10 October 2026, as protesters gathered in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the disputed Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, this distance acquired a material form. Barricades obstructed routes, police detained protesters, and restrictions on transport and mobile internet affected the city’s circulation. The Election Commission maintained that electoral revision was intended to improve the accuracy of voter lists; critics questioned its implementation and warned of possible disenfranchisement. The disagreement was therefore not simply about a list of names. It concerned the conditions under which people could make claims about their own political existence-and whether the institutions responsible for administering citizenship could be held publicly accountable for the ways in which they did so.

This disorientation is followed by anger and confusion, of the body as much as the mind, which coagulate into a mixture of disbelief and reluctant familiarity. We have become accustomed to seeing democracy represented through the visual grammar of elections: the inked finger, the queue outside a polling booth, the electronic voting machine, the triumphant party headquarters. The ballot is photographed; the voter is counted; the result is announced. But what happens when citizens attempt to question the procedures through which the electorate itself is constituted? Who gets to count the people who count? The question sounds like a riddle, but its consequences are administrative, material and profoundly political. When a revision of electoral rolls is contested, the dispute concerns not only the accuracy of a database but also the relationship between documentary legibility and the right to participate. A person may exist socially, work, pay rent, raise children and belong to a neighbourhood, yet still find that their political existence depends upon whether their name appears in the appropriate column. James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) helps explain how governments make complex populations administratively legible through standardised records, categories and measurements. Such legibility is indispensable to many public functions, including the maintenance of electoral rolls. But a list is never the population itself; it is a representation of the population, constructed through rules that can be examined, challenged and corrected. The democratic question is not whether electoral lists should be accurate. Of course they should. It is whether the procedures used to make them accurate are themselves sufficiently transparent, accessible and accountable to those whose political standing depends on them.

How is one to draw space in place of the barricade? Henri Lefebvre’s The Production of Space (1974) offers a useful starting point, because it refuses to treat space as an innocent container into which social life simply pours. Space is produced through power, labour, planning and everyday practice. A road is not merely a road: it is a worker’s route to a shift, a vendor’s access to customers, a commuter’s connection between home and employment, and, under particular circumstances, a place where citizens assemble to make a claim upon the state. The barricade brings these otherwise overlapping uses into conflict. It announces that the road is public, but that its publicness can …

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: 500,000 hectares of Mindanao forest lands up for privatization
content:
The Musuan Peak in Bukidnon. Photo by Franck Dick Rosete/Bulatlat

More than 500,000 hectares of public forest lands in Mindanao are up for investment, a recent report from the national government revealed, raising concerns among Indigenous peoples.

Joselin Marcus Fragada, Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) Undersecretary for field operations and line bureaus, said during this year’s Mindanao Development Forum held in Davao City on October 28 that 500,011 hectares of Mindanao forest lands—excluding in the Bangsamoro region—have been delineated for private investments related to agroforestry, industrial timber and wood processing, and pasture management.

Thirty-five percent of the total lands belong to the Caraga region, followed by the Davao region with 28.8 percent—reportedly considered two of the country’s richest areas in terms of natural resources.

Moreover, on top of these lands, the agency also reported that 132,896 hectares of forest lands in Mindanao were qualified for clean energy projects.

Sabokahan Youth, a group of young Lumad, expressed strong opposition to DENR’s plan. Apart from possibilities that it may affect ancestral domains of Indigenous communities and may result in the increase of land disputes, the group stressed that privatizing forest areas may lead to environmental destruction.

“We challenge the DENR to be sincere in serving the people instead of destroying the environment,” the group said in a statement, also decrying the Mindanao Development Authority’s plan of exploring options for Mindanao to supply production inputs, including raw minerals, the United States-led Pax Silica initiative if it becomes operational.

Read: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica?

The said DENR program will be governed under the Sustainable Forest Land Management Agreement (SFLMA), a production sharing deal between the agency and a qualified applicant to undertake sustainable forest management under a renewable 25-year contract.

DENR Administrative Order No. 2025-22, or the rules and regulations governing SFLMA, shall cover forest lands outside protected areas that are suitable and available for development and utilization.

One of the requirements to be obtained by an applicant is a certificate of non-overlap (CNO), a certification issued by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) attesting that a subject area does not overlap with any ancestral domain.

Fragada said the national government needs the private sector for the state to provide better programs in the country’s timberland and forest land areas.

Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment, in an earlier statement, denounced the SFLMA policy, describing it as a blatant handover of the nation’s forests to profit-driven corporations.

“[It] only deepens the threat to Indigenous and rural poor communities, especially in Mindanao, where intensified Lumad killings are already linked to resource plunder and militarized land grabs,” it added.

Special Archives: Lumad Killings

For the environmental group, such a policy, without a genuine national industrialization that could process the country’s resources for the benefit of the Filipinos, only deepens exploitation and the nation’s dependence on foreign markets. (RVO)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Angry farmers dump rotten vegetables at DA
content:
Vegetable farmers from the Cordillera dumped rotten vegetables at Department of Agriculture’s (DA) main office in Quezon City on Tuesday, protesting the agency’s failure to solve the worsening crisis faced by local food producers.


The protesters said plummeting farm gate prices and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs have forced many farmers in the upland region to refuse farming or selling their produce at bottom level prices.


Farmers led by the Kanatengan Network, Apit Tako, the Cordillera Peoples Alliance (CPA), and KATRIBU are demanding fair floor prices, affordable agricultural inputs, sufficient subsidies, improved farm-to-market roads, measures against vegetable importation and smuggling, and an end to usurious lending and excessive land rental costs.


“The rotten vegetables thrown at the agency were the very same produce that farmers could no longer sell amid intensifying competition with imported vegetables, plummeting farm gate prices, and continuously rising costs of agricultural inputs,” KATRIBU in a statement said.


The Indigenous Peoples’ group said the agriculture department allowed local farmers struggling to recover production costs and earn a decent livelihood.


“Instead of strengthening domestic agricultural production through genuine agrarian reform, adequate government support, and the development of local industries, the Marcos Jr. administration continues to allow agricultural importation and smuggling to undermine Filipino farmers. Local producers are left competing with cheaper imported vegetables while receiving inadequate support to sustain their own production,” the group said.


On Tuesday, the Bureau of Customs announced a planned investigation of a P524.27 million worth of reportedly smuggled agricultural products found in a warehouse in Valenzuela City last October 17. Tons of red onions, beans and legumes, ginger and carrots, as well as peanut products were allowed to pass through customs inspection and were seized outside port premises.


While Cordillera farmers complain of diving farm gate prices, meanwhile, retail prices for their produce have risen in lowland wet markets.

author: groundxero
title: 544 Scientists and Researchers Stand with Siang Valley Anti-Dam Movement; Demand Halt to Mega Project and Release of Detained Activists
content:
“We stand with the people of the Siang Valley in their struggle to protect their river, their lands, their rights and the ability to determine their future. We recognise that the people who call this valley home must have the primary say in determining its future.”


 


Groundxero

 Desk


 


In a strong show of solidarity with the indigenous Adi communities resisting the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) in Arunachal Pradesh, a group of 544 scientists, researchers, and concerned citizens working in the fields of nature, wildlife, society and the environment has called on the Union and state governments to immediately halt all pre-feasibility activities, withdraw additional security forces from the valley and release anti-dam protesters detained and arrested under the stringent Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA).


 


The statement, issued on November 9, 2026, comes amid growing resistance in the Siang Valley to the proposed mega-dam and reports of intensified security deployment, restrictions on people’s movement, arrests and the use of force against protesters.


 


The signatories, many of whom have worked in Arunachal Pradesh and the Eastern Himalayas, describe the Siang Valley as an ecologically irreplaceable landscape of immense biodiversity, cultural significance and traditional knowledge. Referring to an earlier statement by 114 scientists issued on June 9, 2025, they point out that 48 new species and 140 new distribution records have been documented in the valley in the past 15 years alone.


 


The statement warns that large-scale construction in an ecologically fragile and highly seismically active river system could have irreversible consequences. It emphasises that the Siang River, its forests and surrounding mountains sustain not only rich biodiversity but also the livelihoods, cultural identity and traditional knowledge systems of indigenous Adi communities.


 


The scientists express particular concern over the Arunachal Pradesh government’s continued efforts to push ahead with the project’s Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) despite sustained opposition from affected communities. They condemned the militarisation of this otherwise peaceful region, restrictions on movement, arrests and detentions of local anti-dam activists, and the use of tear gas and force against protesters. They also denounce the alleged harassment and intimidation of lawyers, journalists and others standing in solidarity of the movement.


 


Invoking the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP), the signatories assert that the project must not proceed without the free, prior and informed consent of the affected indigenous communities, whose lands, livelihoods, cultural heritage and relationship with the Siang are at stake. They also stressed on the constitutional guarantees of freedom of speech, expression and peaceful assembly.


 


The statement calls on the Arunachal Pradesh and Union governments to stop all PFR-related activities, withdraw additional armed forces from the region, release those detained for participating in the movement, and initiate an open and meaningful dialogue with the affected communities.


 


The signatories affirm that the people who have protected and sustained the Siang Valley for generations must have the primary say in determining its future.


 


The full statement along with the list of signatories is published below:


 


November 9, 2026


 


We, a group of scientists, researchers, conservation practitioners and concerned citizens, many of whom have worked in Arunachal Pradesh and in the Eastern Himalaya, stand in unequivocal solidarity with the people of the Siang Valley in their opposition to the proposed 11,000 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP).


 


The Siang Valley is not merely a site for a proposed mega-infrastructure project. The Siang River, its forests and the surrounding mountains sustain extraordinary biodiversity, livelihoods, traditional knowledge systems and the cultural identity of indigenous Adi communities.


 


A statement issued by a collective of 114 scientists on 9th of June 2025, noted that the Siang is a rich living landscape of immense ecological, cultural and biological significance. In the past 15 years alone, there have been 48 new species described, as well as 140 new distribution records from the valley.

author: Czyrene Farrales
title: Ang mga bata, ang kanilang sining, at ang kanilang pakikisangkot sa lipunan
content:
I believe the children are our future

Itanong mo sa mga bata, ano ang kanilang nakikita sa buhay na hawak nila? – Asin

Malamang ay bata. Iisipin nating wala silang pakialam sa kapaligirang ginagalawan nila. Na ang tanging ginagawa nila sa maghapon ay maglaro sa malawak na lupain sa kanilang Sitio, o kaya nama’y pumilas ng dahon sa mga puno, o ang magtampisaw sa ilog.

Malamang ay bata. Musmos at walang kamuwang-muwang silang nabubuhay sa mundo. Ngunit kung tutuusin, isa sila sa dapat tinatanaw para sa isang kinabukasan.

Sumama ako sa grupo ng mga kabataan para makipamuhay sa isang sitio sa probinsya ng Tarlac. Mahabang oras ang ginugol namin sa byahe bago namin marating ang lugar nang tanghaling tapat.

Ito ang sumalubong sa amin sa Sitio Binyayan, Brgy. O’Donnell sa Capas.

Ang Sitio Binyayan ay nakapaloob sa 9, 450 hectares na lupain sa dating Green CIty na kalauna’y tinawag na New Clark City. Bahagi rin ito ng 1, 600 hectares sa ambisyosong proyektong Pax Silica Hub sa Capas, Tarlac.

Dalawang araw lamang ang aming pananatili sa lugar kung kaya’t kailangan imaksimisa ang paggamit ng oras at panahon para sa mabungang pananaliksik at integrasyon sa mga naninirahan sa Sitio Binyayan..

Sa hapon ay nag-ikot kami sa ilang kabahayan, bago sa gabi naman ay naglaan ng oras para sa kultural na mga aktibidad.

Bahagi sa mga isinagawang aktibidad ang coloring activity na dinaluhan ng iba’t ibang mga kabataan. Isa ako sa naatasang manguna para dito. Marahil gawa rin ng kasanayan ko sa paglikha ng mga dibuho at sining biswal ay malugod kong ginampanan ang tungkulin.

Sa pagsusuyod namin sa komunidad para maghanap ng mga kalahok sa naturang aktibidad, unang lumapit sa akin si Raychelle. Nag-aya pa siya ng ibang mga kabataan, hanggang sa dumami na sila. Mabilis lamang silang yayain– gawa na rin siguro ng wala gaanong akses sa mga aktibidad tungkol sa sining ang lugar.

Makukulit. Maiingay. Hindi maiiwasan at natural sa katangian bilang bata. Ngunit kahit papaano, marunong silang makinig: kung kailan tatahimik, kung kailan sasagot.

Sa simula ay nagpakilala muna kami at dahilan ng aming pananatili sa kanilang komunidad. Mabilis naman nilang naunawaan ang kalagayan.

Wala pa kaming binabanggit ukol sa Pax Silica– pero isang bata agad ang nakasambit ng salitang ito. Nang marinig ko ang sinabi niya, namangha ako. Hindi pala lingid sa kaalaman ng mga bata ang usapin ng Pax Silica.

Kanya-kanya nilang mga sagot. Iba’t iba at alam nila mismo ang epekto sa kanila ng itatayong proyektong malapit sa komunidad nila.

Binigyan namin sila ng paksa para mapakita nila ang kanilang paglalarawan at pag-intindi sa kung paano pangalagaan ang kalikasan.

Lumikha sila ng dibuho. Dibuhong puno ng berde at asul.

Nakita ko ang repleksyon ng paligid namin. Ang malawak na sakahan at bundok na pinapaligiran ang Sitio Binyayan. Ang asul na kalangitan at araw na bumubuhay sa mga pananim. Ang ilog kung saan kumukuha ng patubig para sa irigasyon ang mga magsasaka.

Dito ay mas naunawaan ko ang mga bata.

Kilala nila ang kanilang sitio bilang isang masaganang lupain. Payak man ang buhay ay nagagawa pa rin nilang ngumiti. Subalit sa likod ng mga ngiting ito ay ang pangangamba sa kanilang katiyakan sa kinalakihang komunidad.

Sa aming pagbisita, tumambad sa amin ang ilang bahagi ng dating sakahan na sinimulan nang sementuhin ng BCDA para sa itinatayong kalsada na bahagi ng New Clark City. Maging ang mga itinuturing na sagradong burial grounds ng mga katutubo ay pinatag na para sa naturang daan. Sa tagong lugar rin sa Sitio Binyayan ay may itinatayong pumping station para sa Pax Silica Hub na nakakaapekto sa kanilang pinagkukunan ng tubig sa mga poso.

Kalsada na ang dating mga sakahan

Burial grounds na ginagawang kalsada

Masdan mo ang mga bata, ang aral sa kanila makukuha – Asin

Bagama’t musmos at tila walang kamuwang-muwang sa mundo ay nagagawa nang makisangkot ng mga kabataan. Ang kanilang mga ibinahaging mga sagot ay ang nakikita nilang magiging buhay na hawak nila sa takdang panahon.

Wala sa edad ang pag-unawa sa isyung kinakaharap ng lipunan. Ang kanilang kaalaman, sa kabila ng kamusmusan, kaugnay sa proyektong itatayo sa kanilang komunidad ay isang patunay na hindi sila hiwalay sa laban.

Dahil para sa kanila ang lupa, ang katubigan, ang kalangitan, ang nayon at kapatagan, at maging ang laban para sa isang kinabukasang malaya.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Ahead of Elections, China Turns on Diplomatic Pressure on Taiwan in Lithuania, Pakistan, and Papua New Guinea
content:
THE TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT has announced that Taiwan will soon close its diplomatic office in Papua New Guinea. This occurs after the country set a deadline for all Taiwanese diplomatic staff to leave the country. As Taiwan does not officially have diplomatic relations with Papua New Guinea, the office is technically not an embassy, but a representative office.

The announcement was made unilaterally by Papua New Guinea in July. In response, Taiwan stated that it would suspend purchases of liquefied natural gas from Papua New Guinea, and that it would be shutting down its representative office.

It is unclear whether the move occurs at Papua New Guinea’s initiative or if it is a move aimed at shoring up ties with China. This, too, has been questioned in other incidents in which countries abruptly announced the downgrading of diplomatic representation by Taiwan or other measures, such as revoking overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines.

Indeed, in the past month, Pakistan announced that it would be revoking overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines EVA Air and China Airlines, before later reversing course on the move. It, too, is unclear whether the move occurred at Pakistan’s initiative, perhaps as a means of signalling alignment with China, or if China’s will led to the act–as well as why Pakistan reversed course.

It, too, is possible that international pressure led Pakistan to back down from its decision to revoke overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines. But one notes that Seychelles, Mauritius and Madagascar previously revoked overflight privileges for President Lai Ching-te’s airplane in April, preventing Lai from traveling to Eswatini for a celebration of King Mswati III’s 40th accession to the throne and birthday. At the time, the Taiwanese government asserted that China had threatened to revoke debt cancellation for the countries if they did not comply. Eswatini is Taiwan’s last remaining diplomatic ally in Africa, although it is an authoritarian monarchy ruled by an absolute monarch, with Taiwan providing infrastructure and financial support to the country despite the fact that free elections are forbidden and protests calling for democracy are put down by force.

Likewise, South Africa previously attempted to push Taiwan’s representative office out of the capital of Pretoria in April 2024, which was, too, seen as perhaps an attempt by China to pressure Taiwan’s diplomatic representation abroad. Taiwan initially responded through threats to suspend semiconductor exports to South Africa before backing down. The issue remains unresolved, even if Taiwan does not appear to have been forced to move its representative office. It is unclear if South Africa may resume a push to evict the representative office down the line.

More recent reports suggest that Taiwan has also faced pressure to rename its diplomatic offices in Lithuania, with a Lithuanian media outlet reporting that the Lithuanian government had requested Taiwan to do so. Taiwan’s representative office was opened in Lithuania in 2021, as a sign of warming ties between the two countries, though a shift in the political climate may have resulted in shifts. Taiwan was reportedly requested to change the name of its diplomatic office by October 1st, which is Chinese National Day. For its part, the Taiwanese government has stated that it has no plans to do so.

Otherwise, the Taiwanese government has been reassured of continued ties with Paraguay after the resolution of Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, following a scandal about the collapse of a bank. Peña will be succeeded by Vice President Pedro Alliana, who belongs to the same Colorado Party as Peña. Still, as with Eswatini, one notes that Paraguay and its dominance by the Colorado Party for decades is another case in which Taiwan maintains diplomatic ties with countries that have a questionable human rights record, solely for the purpose of maintaining diplomatic allies abroad. Paraguay has seen the Colorado Rule for 77 years, and there have been reports in the past of Paraguay demanding funding for projects in exchange for recognition.

The timing of these various moves, seemingly intended to constrain Taiwan’s diplomatic space, is suspicious, given that they take place shortly before elections later this month. Though there is no smoking gun to confirm that China is behind these various moves that constrain Taiwan’s diplomatic space, one generally suspects that this is, in fact, a move …

author: Mekong Review 2
title: The death of a scammer Tonggo Simangunsong
content:
Poipet, near the Thailand–Cambodia border. Credit: wattana / Shutterstock.com I t was the end of 2024. Almost five months after losing his job at a food and beverage company, thirty-nine-year-old Rasdy Fawzi told his wife, Kiki Tresia Ginting, that he was going to accept a job in Cambodia. Kiki was concerned, and for good reason. The man who’d offered him the job was part of a scam syndicate; the recruitment agency was unregistered and the work Fawzi would be undertaking was illegal. She’d heard stories of young Indonesians trapped in Cambodia, tortured and forced to work as scammers. “I worried and asked my husband about his safety if he worked there, but he said, ‘That’s okay, it’s fine, don’t worry’,” she recalls. Fawzi reassured her many times that his friend had been there, too, and he trusted him. He believed that he was too old for any company in Indonesia to want to hire him for the same role he’d had in mobile sales marketing with his previous employer. While going to Cambodia was risky, the salary offered would be more than enough to support their small family. It was an opportunity he didn’t want to pass up. author: Kerry Smith
title: Socialist Alliance: Funding cuts to Villamanta throw people with disability on scrap heap
content:
Brenden Grull, Socialist Alliance spokesperson and candidate for Geelong, has called for funding cuts to Villamanta, Geelong’s Disability Rights Legal Service, to be reversed.

The community-based service, which is housed in Geelong West but works across Victoria, fights for the rights of people with disability-related justice issues. It has been operating since 1990.

The Department of Health and Ageing said on November 10 that it would be cutting approximately 30% of Villamanta’s total funding and around 50% of its core funding.

“It is almost unbelievable that as the demand for disability advocacy increases and in defiance of the Disability Royal Commission’s recommendations to recognise independent advocacy as a vital safeguard for people with disability that Villamanta’s funds are being cut so significantly,” Grull told Green Left.

“I understand that the decision will have an immediate impact; it will lead to substantial job losses. I presume that this is part of the federal government’s cuts to NDIS services.

“It is particularly shocking when independent reviews have recognised that Villamanta is a leader in best-practice disability advocacy and community legal support.”

Grull said the cuts will “only cause more pain and suffering for clients and workers”. He said as cost of living pressures rise for everyone, these cuts show federal Labor’s “diminishing commitment” to community-based organisations.

“Labor’s preference is for dodgy providers from the private sector.”

Grull said Socialist Alliance backs Villamanta’s campaign to get the funding cuts reversed and to protect access to independent disability advocacy.

“We support the reintroduction of publicly-funded disability services to fix gaps in the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Villamanta has our 100% support and we will be doing everything in our power to help restore its funding.”

author: Jordan Humphreys
title: The “two souls” of the Spanish general strike
content:
A 24-hour general strike is set to take place across the Spanish state on 11 November, sparked by recent struggles over housing. In the lead-up to the general strike, 

Red Flag

’s 

Jordan Humphreys

 spoke to Germán 

P. Montañés

, a member of the revolutionary organisation Anticapitalistas, about the unfolding situation.

Red Flag

:

 Rising rents and house prices are affecting people across the globe. Why has it become such a flashpoint in the Spanish state in particular? What is the housing situation like there?

Germán

 

P. Montañés:

 Housing in the Spanish state has been a structural problem for a long time. One of the most visible impacts of the 2008 financial crisis was a wave of mortgage evictions. Today, mortgage-related evictions are less common, but renting has become much more widespread.

Even so, renting remains less common in Spain than in cities like Berlin or New York, where tenant voting blocs have played a major political role. In Spain, home ownership is the norm even among much of the working class. This stems from a strategy popularised during the dictatorship—echoing Margaret Thatcher’s later policies in the UK—summarised by a government minister’s famous quote: “I want a country of homeowners, not proletarians”. This high level of home ownership has somewhat cushioned the crisis; without it, the social situation likely would have collapsed much sooner.

Still, the crisis remains severe for two main groups: young people, who are locked out of home ownership and forced to pay exorbitant rents; and low-income workers and migrants, who face the worst housing instability.

The modern housing movement began around 2008 with anti-eviction campaigns such as the Plataforma de Afectados por la Hipoteca (PAH). Later, tenants’ unions emerged from these struggles—founded in 2017 in hubs like Madrid and Barcelona, and expanding across the Spanish state over the past few years.

A major tipping point occurred in late September, when police evicted 87-year-old María del Carmen (Maricarmen) Abascal from her home in Madrid. She had lived there for nearly 50 years under a rent-controlled agreement, but after an investment fund bought the building, her rent drastically increased. On the fourth attempt, police successfully removed her. This high-profile eviction sparked widespread outrage across the country. In response to the growing public backlash, the prime minister brought the general elections forward to 29 November.

RF

: 

Could you give us a better idea about the tenants’ unions—what kind of organisations are they, and what relationship do they have with the revolutionary left?

GPM:

 The emergence of tenant unions reflects the limits of the previous housing movement, which focused almost exclusively on stopping evictions. The problem with focusing on evictions is that the movement arrives far too late: by the time a family is facing removal, the police are already at the door.

The founding principle of the tenants’ unions was to adapt the most effective elements of trade unions to housing—arriving early to conflicts and organising people sooner. Rather than a diffuse social movement, housing activism needed a formal union. Members pay a monthly contribution, providing a financial base that allows staff to work full time and maintains an ongoing presence.

They also drew heavily on US labour tactics, focusing on entire buildings or properties owned by the same investment fund or landlord family to intervene long before eviction day.

They’ve been very successful recently in Madrid. Around September, they had about 2,000 to 3,000 members, and over the last two months of conflict, that number doubled to roughly 6,000. To clarify: these are financial members, not dedicated militants—there are perhaps 100 to 150 core militants—but the growth is significant.

The mainstream political left has no militant presence inside these spaces and does not control them; it tries to exert influence from the outside through government institutions and political pressure.

The revolutionary left isn’t broadly present either, though our organisation is the only one with a real foothold inside the unions. Our influence extends beyond raw numbers: we’ve maintained a dialogue with the union leadership for ten years. While the leaders come from autonomist or anarchist traditions, key militants in leadership positions allow us to maintain a solid presence. Our goal is to build a revolutionary current inside the …

author: John Mullen
title: France: The brass band and the revolution
content:
For the third time in a week, there were major strikes in education and mass demonstrations across France, on November 10.

More than a million people took to the streets in more than 200 towns and cities, on November 5, in support of school students and to demand wage rises, more jobs and an end to cuts in public service budgets. Health workers, dockers, teachers, journalists, municipal staff, train drivers, bank workers and many others joined the one-day strike.

Two days later, hundreds of thousands marched again.

Student assemblies attracted more than a thousand participants at many universities, including Marseille, Rennes, Bordeaux and Paris-Cité.

In some towns, notably Rennes and Bordeaux, and in sectors such as university staff and healthcare, general assemblies of workers (known as interpros or coordinations) are taking the lead in organising the struggle, hoping to overcome the horrific inertia of the national union leaderships.

High school student representatives walked out of a government consultation session on university admissions policy, held in Paris on Monday November 9, when they discovered that ministers had invited fascist MPs to take part.

There are three strands to the present revolt.

First, highschool and university students are in their sixth week of blockades, and are not giving up despite the police beating thousands and mutilating dozens.

Secondly, the Yellow Vest networks are back, and they worry the government because they seem leaderless and prefer wildcat demos.

Most importantly, there is the workers’ movement, which holds, in strike action, our most powerful weapon, but which is held back by catastrophic national leadership from a band of professional “Bordeaux and sandwiches” negotiators.

On the demonstrations, people wave thousands upon thousands of home-made cardboard placards, with slogans from the bawdy to the philosophical, quoting poets, rappers or constitutional documents.

My favourites include: “Let’s do a poo on the fascists!”, “You thirst for power, we thirst for beauty!”, “Class struggle begins in high school!”, “Looters in hoodies make you angry? Looters in suits are your government !”, “Plan A: protest in a dignified manner. Plan B: smash everything up.”, “Have you forgotten how we became a democracy?” and “This is getting expensive in cardboard!”.

The now traditional demo song rings out across the country: “For the honour of the workers, and to build a better world! Although Macron doesn’t like it, here we are!”

Brass bands and orchestras are present everywhere, following a call from the New World Orchestra, who were tear-gassed while playing in mid-October. They have popularised a new demo song: “I’ve two great loves: the brass band and the revolution! Long live blockades and sabotage, occupations and wildcat demos!” Groups of thousands were filmed singing this and dancing.

Last week, a new opinion poll found that 57% of the population approves of the movement, and 88% consider the demands concerning purchasing power and the cost of living legitimate, while 75% approve of the students’ demands. This is impressive, given the massive government propaganda campaign against the revolt.

With such support, even the mainstream media feel obliged to feature interviews with inspiring high schoolers, explaining their demands in detail, even if the channels rapidly return to their preferred fare — interviews with headmasters, police and shopkeepers upset by the movement, and political experts who want to discuss supposed personality clashes between left politicians.

This crisis is not going to go away. Emmanuel Macron’s minority government must push its national budget through before Christmas. Massive tax cuts for the rich mean they are short of money, so their initial proposal is for €50 billion in budget cuts. The international bankers are breathing down their necks, already charging France more than neighbouring countries to borrow money.

The situation is extremely fluid. The government met with unions and bosses on November 9, and then declared that the national minimum monthly wage would be raised — by €24. The CGT union demand is for a €150 rise. Later this week a decision will be announced about public sector wages. Public servants have lost 20% of their purchasing power since 2010, and nearly a million are on the minimum wage.

The national union leaders are following their habitual hymn sheet of “days of action”. The dynamism of Thursday’s social …

author: Jerome Small
title: Carroll’s royal commission: an attack on effective unionism in Victoria
content:
The Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria was announced by Victoria’s Labor Premier Ben Carroll in August: his first act as the incoming premier. 

Carroll’s announcement was a response to a years-long media campaign against the CFMEU, the main construction union. It was also part of a wholesale lurch to the right by an already neoliberal Labor government. And it is a blatant attack on any idea that unions should act to raise wages. 

If proof is needed, just look at the first day of the current bloc of hearings. I attended the first day of the commission back in September and sat through the proceedings yesterday via livestream.  

Literally the main point of yesterday’s hearing was how terrible it was that the CFMEU stopped a major construction job—the Gap Road level crossing removal in Sunbury—for a day and a half in June 2022, and that this resulted in traffic controllers winning an increase in wages from the award rate (at that time $26 per hour) to around $49 per hour. 

The horror. This equates to a full-time wage of $1,862 per week, slightly above Australia’s average full-time wage of $1,835 in 2022. It’s an OK wage, though no king’s ransom. With allowances, shift and casual loading, and the plentiful overtime that construction sites run on, this can add up to a decent wage if you’re prepared to work long hours.

To listen to Chris Young, the counsel assisting the royal commission, a union winning this sort of wage for a blue-collar worker through industrial action in 2026 is a threat to all that is right in the world. So much so that two weeks of the royal commission’s rather expensive time is being devoted to investigating how this could possibly have come about, with the express intention of ensuring it never happens again. 

Young spent yesterday sifting through the circumstances leading up to this supposed affront to decency. The CFMEU had a lot going in its favour. 

Railway crossing removals happen on a tight timetable, planned up to a year in advance. The two companies doing the work—John Holland and CPB—wanted to deliver the job on time in order to secure further work. The labour market was tight in Victoria. The CFMEU had already been successful in securing enterprise agreements with most of the big companies doing this sort of work in Victoria. From the evidence led by counsel assisting, it sounds like the CFMEU judged the moment perfectly—just like any union which is serious about taking action to raise wages should, and historically has. 

Both the CFMEU and the Australian Workers’ Union (AWU) cover workers working on civil construction projects like level crossing removals, and since 2014 the CFMEU has been trying to expand its coverage at the expense of the AWU. The Victorian Labor government at that time was uninterested in helping the AWU maintain coverage over these jobs—like Gap Road—and over traffic control work in particular. 

This was a positive for the workers at Gap Road, and more broadly. The royal commission was told that Zoom Recruitment, one of the AWU-aligned labour hire companies providing traffic control at Gap Road, was operating on a long-expired enterprise agreement that paid only the legal minimum specified in the construction award. 

This is utterly consistent with the business model of the AWU for the past century or more in construction, which is to undercut the wages and condition of the CFMEU and its predecessor unions. And to their credit, for most of that time, the CFMEU and their predecessors generally ignored the AWU’s claims to coverage on “civil” infrastructure work (roads, rail, bridges and tunnels).

The commission heard yesterday that the Labor government’s largely hands-off attitude to this demarcation dispute in 2022, which effectively favoured the CFMEU over the AWU, may have been because of factional alignments within the ruling Labor Party. This is hardly a crime, or even a novel tactic in Australian union politics.  

The AWU has used exactly the same approach, of translating political clout in the Labor Party into industrial coverage (and vice-versa), for its entire existence. The conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Union (SDA) follows the same path. The only difference is that the AWU and the SDA have an appalling record of lifting wages—in fact the SDA did the opposite, helping employers undercut legal minimums, until a path-breaking legal case in the Fair Work …

author: Kerry Smith
title: Students organise nationwide rallies against artificial intelligence
content:
A student-led national day of action against artificial intelligence (AI) and mega data centres was held on November 10. The rallies were called by Students for AI Regulation (SAR), a group of high school and university students, and supported by the Tomorrow Movement.

SAR said students are “terrified of the impact AI is going to have on our future”. “It’s easy to wallow in AI news and climate disasters but … we must act now!”

Speakers at the Gadigal Country/Sydney rally highlighted successful campaigns against AI data centres in Arncliffe, Lane Cove and the Blue Mountains, and called on people to join the December 5 statewide rally against data centres.

Paddy Gibson from Stop the Cooks River AI Project said defeating the project was an important win for people power. He said the fight is not over, as the community wants to stop the developer Stockland’s other plans for the former Kogarah Golf Club site.

Gibson said students and staff at universities and schools are raising important anti-AI demands and cited the National Tertiary Education Union’s push to include AI protection clauses in enterprise agreements.

Robin, a student at the University of New South Wales, high school teacher and campaigner with Students Hate AI, said it was being forced on teachers and students.

Isaac Nellist from Sydney Students for Climate detailed the climate impacts of mega data centres, including their use of vast amounts of electricity and water, and thereby helping the continued expansion of coal and gas mining projects.

“The huge amount of money being invested into AI and AI infrastructure around the world is money that should be going into addressing the existential threat of climate change, and the countless other social issues that we are facing.”

He said data centres were being used to “accelerate militarism and war, drive down wages and workers rights and replace artists and steal their work”, while driving inflation and pushing up the cost-of-living.

“AI is a key part of the AUKUS pillar two agreement, which further ties Australia to the US military … and we are seeing the devastating impacts of AI-enabled warfare in Gaza and Iran.

“The good news is that communities are fighting back, we know data centres are massively unpopular and when communities organise and fight back, they win.”

About 80 people joined the Naarm/Melbourne rally at the State Library of Victoria. Jacob Andrewartha, childcare worker and Socialist Alliance candidate for Pascoe Vale, said AI is a “technology that represents the destruction of the environment and an attack on our democratic rights”.

He said AI was being used in surveillance and by government agencies. “There isn’t a convincing case for why we should use AI … What does it have to offer? Worse artistic works? Polluting social media?

“Young people are rejecting this technology, despite the massive investment from big tech capitalists.”

Rallies were also held in Garamilla/Darwin, Nipaluna/Hobart, Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, Kanamaluka/Launceston, Magan-djin/Brisbane and Kabi Kabi Country/Sunshine Coast.

author: Odessa Bishop-McMurray
title: “If they won’t give us a future, we will build one right here” - why the French revolt should inspire high-schoolers everywhere
content:
As one of the organisers of the upcoming nationwide 

Students Say No to Hanson

 demonstration on 12 November, I’ve had to endure a lot of inanity from the media and the right. Amongst snide remarks about the stages of brain development and warnings of the mortal dangers of missing two periods of class, one accusation keeps coming up: that we’re plotting to bring “French-style riots” to Australian cities. 

Right-wing journalists seized on an Instagram post we made on 11 October, conveying the inspiration we draw from French student protesters fighting government austerity and the far right. 

Cue an avalanche of hysterical headlines and news segments: The Murdoch-owned Adelaide 

Advertiser

 warned readers to brace for “walkouts ‘inspired’ by violent French protests”. Pauline Hanson went on Brisbane’s 4BC Radio to rip into us:

“...They are saying they are inspired by what’s going on in France. What? The 

looting

? The 

burning

? The 

destruction

? They’re 

inspired

 by that?”

Well, we’re not sorry for being inspired by French students. Everyone who wants to see a better world should identify with their struggle. 

Young people everywhere are facing a dire future, and revolt is rightly spreading. It’s clear even to some in the establishment that what’s happening in France is part of a global wave of protest with deep roots. As former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown wrote this week in 

The Guardian

: “A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken—and they know it.”

Both far-right governments and “sensible centrists” are taking us on the same trajectory: more racism, more militarism, and more austerity. 

When states aren’t attempting to re-introduce conscription, as in Germany, they’re funnelling billions into the military-industrial complex while schools crumble. In France, students endure classrooms infested with cockroaches, mould and overcrowding, sometimes numbering 35 students to a class. 

We’ll likely never be able to afford secure housing or sufficient healthcare. We’ve watched politicians choose fossil fuel companies over the habitability of our planet. For many of us, the establishment’s unanimous endorsement of Israel’s genocide in Gaza was the final nail in the coffin.

It’s obvious that the journalists’ and politicians’ pearl-clutching about a few broken Parisian shop windows is a means of avoiding discussion of these issues. And their condemnation of violence rings hollow when they decline to comment on the vastly greater violence that the system inflicts on people daily. 

There’s the violence that is inherent in running such an unequal society. French youth linger without a future in the slums while the richest 500 families own nearly half the country. Schools and hospitals in France are crumbling, but the latest budget announcement includes 54 billion euros in further cuts to public spending. The police systematically brutalise Black and Arab working-class migrants. The high-profile killing of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, which sparked a nationwide revolt in 2023, is part of a long history of racialised policing. 

When these injustices generate resistance, there’s one public service the government can guarantee: the bludgeoning of protestors, tear gas, and potentially lethal stun grenades; exploding a student’s hand, breaking another’s jaw and leaving two 16-year-olds blinded for life. 

This is an inherent admission that the ruling class has no genuine plan to improve society. They just want resignation from ordinary people, and when that fails, tear gas is their backup plan.

But French students have shown that resignation gets us nowhere; Our power comes from the streets, and that’s a lesson the ruling class desperately does not want students to learn.

Already, France has shown small glimpses of how these movements can win real gains. While still hoping to crush the movement, the government has already been forced to make concessions. They’ve announced plans to cap class sizes, hire more teachers, and create more university places. This is a tiny fraction of what the movement is demanding, but it proves a timeless truth: a month of rebellion can win more change than decades of asking nicely.

A grassroots student movement in Serbia just ended the 14-year rule of the repressive Vučić regime. In Brazil, thousands of students flocked to the streets to successfully halt the advance of far-right presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.

It seems like …

author: Rachel Evans
title: Anti-racists counter protest far-right ‘Australia Marches’ rally
content:
About 300 people joined the “No to Racism: Migrants and Refugees Are Welcome” rally at Sydney Town Hall on November 8. It was organised by the Refugee Action Collective Sydney (RAC) to counter the far-right Australian Marches rally against migration.

The far-right rally, which featured speakers from One Nation, Libertarian MP John Ruddick and other right-wing influencers, rallied at the Royal Botanic Garden and drew about 500 people.

Speakers at the counter-protest included Lynda-June Coe, Wiradjuri and Badu Island woman and NSW Greens upper house candidate; Nour Salman from Australia Palestine Advocacy Network; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Bidjigal/Gweagal activist Jordan Ryan-Hennessy; Ann El Khoury, from University of Sydney Staff for Palestine; Beau Lyon from Action for Public Housing’ and Anisa, a Somali refugee who was held in the Naoero detention centre.

Chakrabarty spoke about the racism faced by Indian migrants and linked One Nation and the Australia Marches rally to the far-right Narendra Modi government in India.

Ian Rintoul from RAC, who chaired the rally, said the United States midterm elections were a huge blow to the racist politics of US President Donald Trump, but said anti-racist campaigners still need to get organised.

“The tragedy is that the racist policies of Australia Marches and One Nation are being fueled by anti-migration and anti-refugee policies of the Labor government,” Rintoul said.

“Labor is linking migration with the housing crisis; cutting the numbers of international students; has introduced fees that will make it harder for refugees to seek asylum in Australia and is implementing an ICE-like compliance force to round up people on temporary visas.”

Lyon said those in power are pushing racism to distract from the real cause of the housing crisis, the for-profit housing system.

“Migrants are not responsible for the housing or cost of living crisis,” Rintoul said.

author: Sagar Sanyal
title: Emergency and autocracy in Modi’s India
content:
The far-right government in India led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi has been increasingly repressive and anti-democratic over recent months. Commentators are asking if the country is in the grip of an ‘

undeclared Emergency

’, a reference to the 1975-77 period of ‘Emergency rule’ by then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in which activists and trade unionists were simply rounded up and jailed. 

The current repression is a response to the student and youth protests that erupted in the capital, New Delhi, in late July. They were sparked by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), a satirical movement that began on social media a couple of months earlier. The scale and intensity of the protests surprised the regime, as did the mocking anti-Modi tenor of popular chants. While the protest demand was for the resignation of the education minister over exam leaks, the protesters were motivated by visceral opposition to Modi, who has ruled since 2014. The police lashed out using the sort of 

force

 that they typically use in repressed regions like Kashmir. Police fired pellet guns, used nail-studded batons and sexually assaulted women protesters. 

Despite the repression, tens of thousands mobilised daily for five days—high school and university students, middle-class and working-class youth. Not only in Delhi, but in dozens of cities around the country. Alongside clips of police brutality circulating on social media, there are clips of youth chasing police off the streets with their sheer numbers and bravado. There are clips of cheeky middle-class youth approaching police who are away from the heat of the action to ask mocking questions like “Dear Mr. Officer, are you planning to tear gas protesters today?” The government is tracking down incriminating and embarrassing recordings of those events and asking social media platforms to 

remove them

.

Public opinion has turned strongly against Modi’s repression. Among the Hindi-speaking, middle-class, upper-caste Hindus who have been the most secure vote base of the BJP, parents now saw their own children being beaten—just for demanding a fair opportunity in college exams! Ultimately, the administration conceded the protest demand to sack the education minister, a humiliating 

defeat

 for Modi. It gave the lie to the “unstoppable strongman” image of him so carefully crafted by pro-Modi big media. 

Less than three months after the July protests, a new protest movement gripped the nation. It demands the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner of India, Gyanesh Kumar, who has been highly partisan to Modi and his 

Hindu nationalist

 Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and, according to some parties, rigged state elections in Bihar (May 2025) and West Bengal (April 2026). In West Bengal, the BJP won for the first time due in part to the chief election commissioner disqualifying millions of names from the eligible voters list. Deletions disproportionately targeted Muslims, who are an ideological enemy of Hindu nationalists, and who were also an important vote base of the party the BJP displaced—the Trinamool Congress (TMC). 

Following a late September 

expose,

 which revealed that the chief election commissioner had overruled the protestations of even his fellow election commissioners, the CJP and left student groups took up vote-rigging as a national campaign to channel the energy from the July student movement. Demands for the chief election commissioner to resign have been taken up by all opponents of the BJP. 

When a large protest was called for 

10 October

, the state responded by locking down New Delhi. Around 40,000 paramilitary and police laid siege to a sizeable area around the “designated protest site” of Jantar Mantar in the centre of the city. They blocked roads and shut down local internet mobile services (India is 

among the worst

 states for this). They closed over 40 metro train stations in Delhi and stopped over 200 inter-city trains from reaching Delhi. They threatened activists in their homes on the night before the march, this coming on top of regular arbitrary detention of prominent leaders of the protest movement (from the CJP and the left parties). 

Undeterred

, protestors appeared in their tens of thousands and were again met with batons and tear gas, and thousands were detained.

Sizeable protests have continued sporadically since 10 October, some called by the CJP or student organizations of the left, 

others

 by major opposition parties. The …

author: Rick Kuhn
title: Unemployment: a feature of capitalism, not a bug
content:
Today more than one in ten workers can’t find enough paid labour to live a decent life. And that’s only workers actively looking for a job or for more hours of employment. It doesn’t count those who have given up on finding a job, even though they want one, and survive thanks to friends, family or a measly government payment that isn’t an unemployment benefit.

In September

 the seasonally adjusted

un

employment rate was 4.7 percent;

under

employment was 6.3 percent. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, you’re not unemployed if you worked even an hour in the survey fortnight.

To get the Jobseeker Payment or Youth Allowance the un- and underemployed have to follow the Albanese government’s savage eligibility rules, inherited from its Liberal predecessors. If you earn more than a pitiful $75 a week, your payment starts to go down. You must follow the instructions of Workforce Australia and, if you’ve been directed to one, of an outsourced “employment services provider” agency, which profits from government funding.

That may mean applying for a certain number of jobs every “reporting period”, doing training they tell you to do, however meaningless courses about writing job applications or behaviour during an interview might be; or perform “work for the dole”, that would normally be done for much higher award wages. You have to “accept any offer of suitable paid work”, defined by the provider, whether the type of work or its location actually suits you or not.

If you’re single, without kids, the dole is

currently


a princely $413 a week. Certainly in Sydney, you’d be very lucky if less than half of that went on renting a room. And if you’re young, that’s unfortunate: unemployed aged 21 or younger are penalised and get less money than those over 21. Apparently young people don’t need as much shelter, food, clothing, etc. as older people.

Both the unemployment and underemployment rates are rising.

Unemployment is not a bug in capitalism, but a feature. The threat of un- and underemployment – descending into what Marx called “

the industrial reserve army

”—disciplines workers fearful of losing their jobs. The higher the level of unemployment, other things being equal, the less likely they are to take risks by fighting to defend or improve their pay and conditions.

The extent of the reserve army of labour changes in the course of economic cycles: lower during booms, higher in slumps.

Many central banks, like the Reserve Bank of Australia, are bumping up interest rates to slow their countries’ economies down. Their goal is not increased unemployment; that’s a side effect. Their main target is the rate of inflation. High inflation—lack of stability in the purchasing power of money—makes calculations by capitalists about their activities and especially investments more difficult.

In legislation

, the RBA has two goals: “price stability and the maintenance of full employment”. It says that “

[t]hese two objectives usually work together

”. In practice, the bank favours sacrificing jobs to keep a lid on inflation.

But today, high oil prices, due to the USA’s and Israel’s war on Iran, is the main driver of inflation. The RBA isn’t bumping up interest rates to discipline workers, although that’s a side-effect. Governor

Michelle Bullock

said at the end of September that “There is no wage price spiral going on in Australia. Rises in wages are not driving … cost pressures”.

In fact, it is workers who are mainly affected by inflation. Greg Jericho, in the

Guardian

, has illustrated how workers’ real pay has been falling since 2021, compared with the Consumer Price Index by 7 percent; compared with the more appropriate Employee Living Cost Index, by more than 12 percent.

The hostility of most union officials to leading their members in serious struggles to defend, let alone restore or improve their living standards, is mainly to blame.

In his 1972 report

Poverty in Australia

, Ronald Henderson, appointed by the Liberal government of Billy McMahon, calculated a poverty line, marking an “austere” standard of living below which people were in poverty. The Melbourne Institute of Economic Research frequently updates it.

JobSeeker

has consistently been below this line. Today that unemployment benefit is less than half the

Henderson poverty line

. Using 50, let alone 60 percent of median

household income

, common alternative international measures of poverty, the situation of people on JobSeeker …

author: Simon Childs
title: Millions of Workers Shut Down Spain With First General Strike in 14 Years
content:
Spanish workers braved stormy weather to go on general strike in protest against the country’s housing crisis on Wednesday.


Unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers, as millions downed tools three weeks before a snap general election. There were

“total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.


Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector are also taking part, they added. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% are striking while 35% of postal service workers have also joined.


The 24-hour strike, Spain’s first in 14 years, is backed by the country’s two biggest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as tenants’ associations fighting rising rents and evictions.


“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.


Mass protest marches were planned for Wednesday afternoon despite the expected arrival of two storms, Charles and Bruna.


Unions pointed to a 10% drop in electricity demand across the country, saying it shows that activity in energy-intensive industries such as steel processing had come to a halt.


Barcelona’s metro is only running during peak commuting hours. Protesters swarmed Madrid’s municipal bus depot in an attempt to stop busses from moving and dragged wheelie bins into roads in order to stop traffic. Shops in Barcelona were closed in anticipation of unrest.


The CCOO union

said on X

 that 13 people in Madrid needed medical attention after police fired pepper spray at picketers. “It’s a disgrace that workers are being prevented from exercising their right to strike,” the union said.


Spain has witnessed weeks of protests over housing, sparked by the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. 


The country  has a deficit of 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to over a million by 2028. The average rental price of a home – €1,176 – is equivalent to 98.7% of the average young person’s monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain.


The protests have led Spain’s government to call a snap election on 29 November, after it was unable to pass housing reforms in the legislature, where it lacks an outright majority. 


With the far-right ahead in the polls, Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party prime minister Pedro Sanchez is hoping to mobilise his base around the housing crisis despite criticism from protesters that his government has failed to address the issue for years. 


A train c that killed dozens on the high speed line south from Madrid last month – the country’s fourth deadly train crash this year –  has also damaged confidence in Sanchez’s government.

author: Mark Engler
title: Democrats should wield their power to return agency to ordinary people
content:
This article

Democrats should wield their power to return agency to ordinary people

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Too often, we have seen a fundamental asymmetry at work: When Democrats win power, they might pass a modest minimum wage increase. When Republicans are in power, they do things like decimate public sector unions. In the long term, this is an imbalance that leads to ruin. 


Last week’s “blue tsunami” represented a resounding repudiation of the Trump agenda. While it is common that a sitting administration will lose seats in the midterm elections, swings of the magnitude that we have just witnessed are rare and important. For certain, Trump will still try to use the executive branch to wreak havoc on democracy and provide egregious giveaways for  the billionaire class. However, Democratic control of the Senate and the investigatory power of its majority in the House should provide an important check on his ability to do damage. 


Perhaps more importantly, progressive forces made critical gains at the state level. The Democrats

won six new “trifectas”

: in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Now, if current leads in Kansas and Alaska hold, “about 75 percent of Americans will live in states with Democratic governors,” and roughly 53 percent will reside in places where Democrats control both chambers of the state legislature as well,

Newsweek


reports

.


Of course, we should not assume that Democrats will use their newfound power effectively if left to their own devices. There are significant blocs of the Democratic Party wherein centrist politicians have made careers of “playing to the middle” and embracing pro-corporate neoliberal politics. Should this tendency prevail, the Democrats will have squandered a historic opportunity, to the detriment of social movements and the broader American public alike.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Forging an alternative path will mean pushing newly empowered legislators to think and act differently. Passing policies that make a real difference in the lives of working people is critical; however, this is only a first step. For movements for social and economic justice to secure long-term wins, they need to be advocating for how they — and their allies in office — can pursue structural reforms. 


A few years ago, after the 2022 midterms, my brother Paul and I wrote an article

looking at the trifecta power

 that Democrats had gained in multiple states and asking, “Will they actually use it?” More specifically, it asked whether they would use their mandate “to enact changes that increase democratic participation and build progressive power” over the long haul.


When Republicans have gained majorities at the state level “they have used their power to push through reforms that weaken left-leaning constituencies and undermine the Democratic base,” we wrote at the time. “In contrast, when Democrats have been in the majority, they often have failed to reverse these changes or enact meaningful structural reforms — the kind of changes that both improve people’s lives and build power for the grassroots groups that can help them govern on an ongoing basis.” 


Structural reforms can come in many varieties: labor rights, campaign finance issues, measures to encourage and expand voting, redistricting, preemption laws determining whether issues are handled at the state or local level, free speech protections, regulatory modifications that allow for community involvement, and changes to the tort system, to name just a few. More than the specific issue or need addressed by a policy, being attuned to structural reforms means paying attention to how a change gives grassroots forces greater room to maneuver and reach for more in the future.


For social movements, structural reforms are a key mechanism of

inside-outside politics

, through which grassroots organizations work to elect champions into office who then, in turn, use the power of government to strengthen democratic participation and boost outside campaigns for social justice. Unfortunately, the right often has a better understanding of this process than liberals do.


A dramatic example of how Republicans used statewide governing power to alter the balance of forces was how Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, upon gaining a trifecta in 2010, sought to permanently kneecap unions. Recognizing the importance of …

title: Enzo Traverso: “La revuelta juvenil tiene una dimensión política evidente”
content:
Paris 2026: «siamo tutti antifacisti»


https://www.facebook.com/reel/1145355668017795


.


Enzo Traverso: “La revuelta juvenil tiene una dimensión política evidente”


Enzo Traverso

 


06/11/2026


En “Supervivencias de la revuelta”, el historiador pone de relieve la “vida póstuma” de las experiencias emancipadoras, a contracorriente de los relatos nacionales. En una entrevista con Mathieu Dejean para Mediapart, descifra los vínculos subterráneos que unen esta memoria rebelde y el movimiento social actual.


Contra la despolitización y la anestesia del pasado, el historiador Enzo Traverso, profesor de la Universidad de Cornell (Ithaca, Nueva York), revive las memorias rebeldes. Después de 

La melancolía de izquierda 

(2016) y 

Revolución 

(2022), su nuevo libro, 

Supervivencias de la revuelta. Ensayo sobre la dialéctica de la memoria 

(2026) -en francés en las ediciones La Découverte- cierra esta trilogía advirtiendo a los ciudadanos contra las políticas de memoria regidas por las instituciones e invitándolos a apropiarse de la tradición de los oprimidos.


“Esta memoria de las revueltas es subterránea, discreta, pero surge de forma imprevista”, 

escribe. El 17 de octubre de 2026 es una demostración de ello: varias capas de memorias rebeldes se entrecruzaron, desde el 17 de octubre de 1961 en la Comuna de París en 1871. Vuelve, en una entrevista con 

Mediapart

, sobre lo que el movimiento social actual lleva de recuerdos y sobre sus potencialidades, a pesar de la incertidumbre, para finalmente 

“dejar la época contemporánea”.


“Mediapart”: Un alto funcionario de la policía dijo, sobre el 

17 de octubre

: “Era la Comuna de París el día del Black Friday. ¿No es la memoria anti Comuna la que se manifiesta con fuerza desde esa fecha?


Enzo Traverso: 

Hay algo asombroso en la posteridad de la Comuna de París, que tiene tanto el estatus de paradigma para las memorias rebeldes -resurge constantemente, no solo en Francia, sino a escala global- como para el pensamiento reaccionario. Ha proporcionado un repertorio de figuras, referencias, símbolos, imágenes en la cultura reaccionaria, que se ha reactivado constantemente durante un siglo y medio.


De hecho, este es el caso desde el 17 de octubre, no solo en Francia sino también en Italia, donde se invocan los mismos motivos -la civilización amenazada por la barbarie, los salvajes que se apoderan de los centros de las ciudades-, con una dimensión xenófoba y racista particularmente importante. La juventud de los suburbios postcoloniales actúa como un nuevo chivo expiatorio. Un imaginario reaccionario global está tomando forma.


¿Cuáles son las referencias adoptadas precisamente de la memoria anti Comuna?


Si pensamos en la literatura anti Comuna, Théophile Gautier calificó a los protagonistas de la Comuna de París de 

“bestias”, 

“animales apestosos” 

y 

“venenosos” 

escapadas de un zoológico, que hacen estragos en la ciudad porque el guardián se olvidó de cerrar la jaula. Son los mismos clichés que se propagan hoy.


Una gran figura del pensamiento reaccionario de la época, Alphonse Daudet, dijo al día siguiente de la Comuna: 

«¡París estaba en manos de los negros!

 Es una racialización y una animalización de la revuelta y los rebeldes que, en una continuidad asombrosa, perduran hasta nuestros días.


En ambos casos, podemos destacar la negativa de los gobernantes -en este caso Emmanuel Macron, Sébastien Lecornu y Laurent Nuñez- a 

cuestionar las causas sociales y políticas de la revuelta

. Como en la Comuna de París, la revuelta es para ellos un fenómeno mucho más biológico que social. Lo que explica la revuelta es la naturaleza racial o religiosa de los rebeldes, aunque muchos jóvenes blancos fueron muy activos el 17 de octubre. En su imaginación, hay que ver al rebelde como un cuerpo ajeno a la nación.


En términos más generales, parece que el pueblo ha permanecido, en la mente de las élites gobernantes, una “multitud vil”, como dijo Adolphe Thiers.


Esta es una observación interesante, porque lo que también llama la atención es el relativo silencio de la extrema derecha, que a menudo se califica de “populista”. A menudo ha reivindicado la ira legítima de las clases populares contra el 

establishment

, del pueblo virtuoso contra las élites corruptas. Pero a diferencia de 2017 y 2022, Emmanuel Macron se encuentra en tal estado de derrota que Rassemblement national (RN) se ha ganado la confianza de las élites dominantes, de las que se ha …
