author: anred
title: ¿Qué pasó en Guernica?, el gobierno de Alberto y la represión a la última ola de tomas de tierras
content:
Sergio Berni, entonces ministro de Seguridad bonaerense, se jactaba de desalojar cinco tomas de tierra por semana. Era plena pandemia, cientos de miles de familias que no podían pagar alquileres o vivían hacinadas buscaron una salida en la ocupación de terrenos. Ocurría la última gran ola de “tomas de tierras” durante el gobierno de Alberto Fernández que terminó marcada por la represión, las promesas incumplidas y el abandono. Guernica se convirtió en el caso visible y emblemático de aquella crisis: la organización de más de 2 mil familias en tierras “compradas” en dictadura destinadas a un country, la resistencia al desalojo y la exposición mediática obligaron al gobierno provincial a abrir una negociación que estuvo atravesada por titubeos, dilaciones y propuestas que no resolvían el problema habitacional. Por ANRed | Imagen: German Romeo Pena


Primero es necesario contar que la “ocupación de tierras “ tras la dictadura fue una modalidad habitual de las clases trabajadoras más empobrecidas para adquirir sus viviendas ante la sucesiva falta de respuesta habitacional que dieron las democracias posteriores, es decir ni el Estado y menos el mercado resolvieron la crisis habitacional. Para aquel entonces los últimos datos eran delCenso Nacional de 2010, el déficit habitacional alcanzaba 3,5 millones de vivienda entre ellas 1,3 millones de viviendas faltantes y 2,2 millones de viviendas que no proveían  las condiciones mínimas para mantener un nivel de vida digno. 9 millones de personas que eran inquilinos, cifras que actualmente se han agravado en el último censo del 2022.


Luego el desenlace del conflicto en Guernica, disputa que estuvo atravesado por la crisis política y económica que sacudía al gobierno de Alberto Fernández. En septiembre de 2020, la disparada de los dólares paralelos, la presión empresaria y la preocupación oficial por la inestabilidad económica habilitaron una ofensiva política contra las tomas de tierras. Sergio Massa, junto con la intendenta de Presidente Perón, Blanca Cantero, impulsaron una posición de endurecimiento frente a las ocupaciones. Cantero convocó a intendentes del conurbano que reclamaban una respuesta judicial y policial, mientras se consolidaba un bloque político que exigía terminar con la toma y enviar una señal contra nuevas recuperaciones. Guernica comenzaba a ser presentada como un antecedente peligroso que debía clausurarse para evitar que se multiplicara.


14 intendentes piden desalojar tomas de tierras y Berni se publicita defendiendo la «propiedad privada»


La tensión se agravó en octubre con la ocupación de la estancia Casa Nueva, perteneciente a la familia Etchevehere, en Entre Ríos. La iniciativa fue impulsada por Dolores Etchevehere junto al Proyecto Artigas, con el acompañamiento de Juan Grabois y militantes vinculados del Movimiento de Trabajadores Excluidos (MTE), que proponía desarrollar un proyecto agroecológico en esas tierras. La reacción de empresarios y la derecha política que venía presionando por desalojar Guernica reaccionó de inmediato: el conflicto se convirtió en una bandera contra las recuperaciones de tierras y en una supuesta amenaza generalizada a la propiedad privada. La disputa con los Etchevehere intensificó la presión política y mediática sobre el gobierno nacional. Dentro del Frente de Todos también se profundizaron las diferencias: mientras un sector intentaba sostener la negociación y encontrar una salida habitacional, Massa, Berni y los intendentes reclamaban hacer cumplir la orden judicial. Las negociaciones impulsadas inicialmente desde Nación, con participación de funcionarios vinculados al Movimiento Evita, contemplaron una posible relocalización colectiva, pero naufragaron en medio de las disputas internas entre el Movimiento Evita y La Cámpora. Desde septiembre, Andrés Larroque quedó al frente de las conversaciones provinciales, cada vez más condicionadas por la presión judicial y política.


Finalmente, el 28 de octubre, cuando todavía se discutía una última prórroga y existían conversaciones para evitar una intervención violenta, la Justicia rechazó el pedido de postergación y la gobernación cancelo las negociaciones inventando justificaciones. En la madrugada del 29, unos 4.000 efectivos de la Policía Bonaerense.. title: „So kann man nicht mehr leben“: Auch in Portugal wird gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und Wohnungsnot protestiert
content:
Dossier


„

Seit Jahren werden wir durch steigende Immobilienpreise und Lebenshaltungskosten ausgebeutet. Wir arbeiten uns zu Tode und rackern uns ab, um mit unserem Gehalt bis zum Monatsende durchzukommen, die steigenden Kraftstoffpreise und die Grundausgaben zu bewältigen und unsere Wohnung nicht zu verlieren. Uns bleiben nur Schulden und Sorgen, während die Aussicht auf eine bessere Zukunft schwindet.

Coimbra bleibt nicht außen vor! Wir rufen alle dazu auf, sich am kommenden *Mittwoch (14.) ab 17:30 Uhr auf der Praça da República* zu einer Malaktion sowie zum Anbringen eines Transparents und anderer Materialien zu versammeln

.“ portug.

Aufruf zur Demo am 10. Oktober


 der Instagram-Plattform „Não dá mais para viver assim“ („So kann man nicht mehr leben“) und mehr dazu:


In Portugal schließen sich die Kämpfe gegen Lebenshaltungskosten und für öffentliche Infrastuktur zusammen – ein Generalstreik spätestens am 24. November nicht ausgeschlossen 


Portugal: Nach der gewaltsamen Räumung kämpfen neue Protestlager gegen Wohnungsnot und Mietengesetz in Lissabon und Porto auch fürs Demonstrationsrecht


Wohnungskrise in Portugal: Protestcamp oder Weihnachtsmarkt?


„

In Portugal hat die Aktivistin Renata Cambra vor Gericht einen symbolischen Sieg errungen: Ihr Zelt auf einem zentralen Platz in Lissabon darf aufgebaut bleiben. Aber genau dort soll bald der Weihnachtsmarkt stehen. Sie ist zur Symbolfigur der Proteste gegen die Wohnungskrise in Portugal geworden. Die Aktivistin Renata Cambra verbucht einen juristischen Erfolg, denn ihr Zelt auf der Praça do Rossio in Lissabon darf aufgebaut bleiben. Genug Solidarität für ein neues Protestlager gab es zunächst aber nicht. Das Gericht entschied, ihr Zelt sei keine illegale Besetzung des öffentlichen Raums, sondern ein symbolisches Element des Protests. Die Entscheidung beschränkte die Erlaubnis jedoch auf die Demonstrantin, die den Antrag gestellt hat. In dem Verfahren prüfte das Gericht nicht die „Rechtmäßigkeit einer kollektiven Besetzung“ des Rossio oder das Bestehen eines allgemeinen Rechts, „Zelte im öffentlichen Raum durch eine unbestimmte Zahl von Teilnehmern“ zu errichten.


Protestzelt darf auch nachts stehenbleiben


Das Gericht stellte außerdem fest, dass ein Ende der Demonstrationen um 0 Uhr 30 „nicht absolut und automatisch“ ist, und erlaubte Renata Cambra, mit einem Zelt die Nacht über auf der Praça do Rossio zu bleiben.  Der Protest kann dem Gerichtsentscheid zufolge bis zum 24. November 2026 fortgesetzt werden. Das ist der geplante Termin für die Schlussabstimmung über den Staatshaushalt für 2027.


Renata Cambra und die Bewegung „Acampada de Lisboa“ sehen darin einen Sieg für das Demonstrationsrecht in Portugal. (…)


Nach einer gewalttätigen Nacht zum Sonntag, in der es in Lissabon und Porto erneut zu Polizeieinsätzen mit Schlagstöcken kam, blieb die Lage ruhig. Das gewaltsame Vorgehen der Polizei am Wochenende veranlasste den Präsidenten der Republik, António José Seguro, die Regierung und die Ombudsfrau um Aufklärung zu bitten. Ein Anwalt kündigte außerdem eine Strafanzeige wegen Amtsmissbrauchs gegen den Innenminister und den verantwortlichen Polizeidirektor an.


Das Innenministerium (MAI) unterstrich, dass die Entscheidung des Verwaltungsgerichts zu den Wohnungsprotesten die Rechtmäßigkeit der Polizeieinsätze nicht bewerte und kein Recht auf das Aufstellen von Zelten im öffentlichen Raum anerkenne

…“

Artikel von Joana Mourão Carvalho vom 3. November 2026 auf Euronews


 mit Video


Proteste gegen die Wohnungsnot in Portugal


„

Junge Portugiesen haben gegen die Wohnungsnot demonstriert. Lissabons Polizei ging dabei gegen ein Protestcamp vor. Die Regierung will die Mietpreisbremse abschaffen, Zwangsräumungen erleichtern

.“

Portugal Demos gegen Wohnungsnot – Protestcamps geräumt


„

In vielen europäischen Ländern gehen momentan junge Menschen auf die Straße – auch in Portugal. Dort richten sich die Demonstrationen vor allem gegen die Wohnungsnot. Die Polizei ging hart gegen ein Protestcamp in Lissabon vor.

Most of us had jobs, we navigated public transport, looked after younger siblings. We were expected to make informed decisions about our future careers and our sexual partners. We were allowed to leave education and work full time (this was not necessarily good thing - I think increasing the school leaving age to 18 was broadly for the best). Most of us were smoking, or drinking, or both - again, not good things, but just facts - and many of us were sexually active. Many of the AFAB people I knew were on the pill. Legally, we could live independently, or get married with adult consent.

Legally (I live in the UK) we were not minors, although we inhabited an odd legal limbo until we turned 18, and we were certainly not “children”. author: Daron Letts
title: Dialogue about Inuit-specific housing funding underway, says Indigenous Services Minister
content:
Inuit-Nunangat’s share of billions of dollars in federal housing and infrastructure funding announced in

Thursday

‘s budget

 remains undetermined, but that could change soon, Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty said Saturday in Iqaluit.


“I think that we’ll have greater clarity in the next few days,” Gull-Masty said during a news conference at the Inuusirvik Community Wellness Hub. It marked the start of a two-day visit to the territory, her first trip to the eastern Arctic. In addition to her role as Indigenous Services minister, Gull-Masty is the Liberal MP for Abitibi—Baie-James—Nunavik—Eeyou, the sprawling Quebec riding that includes Nunavik.


The Liberal government’s budget allocated $30 billion for First Nations housing and infrastructure as part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new commitment to eliminate homelessness within a decade.


But the budget did not mention comparable investments for Inuit communities.


However, discussions with Inuit organizations about how to fund housing and infrastructure in Inuit communities are ongoing, Gull-Masty said.


“It’s imperative that we take the time, that we take that space and really have that conversation to reflect the uniqueness of the North,” she said. “It’s important for us if we want to reach that target in the North that we shape it according to the realities of what it means to live here and deliver services.”


She met with representatives from Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., the organization that represents Inuit beneficiaries under the Nunavut Agreement, on Saturday.


On Thursday, she met with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed, the head of the national organization for Inuit in Canada.


Gull-Masty said the dialogue about Inuit-specific funding for housing and infrastructure will continue later this year during a meeting of the Inuit-Crown Partnership Committee, a bilateral forum that brings together Inuit leaders and federal cabinet ministers to advance shared priorities.


Nunavut MP Lori Idlout and Iqaluit Mayor Solomon Awa also met with Gull-Masty on Saturday.


Idlout said she is confident Nunavut will be included in Carney’s commitment to eliminate homelessness across Canada within a decade.


“What this government will need to do is make sure that it works respectfully with the Inuit organizations to ensure that Nunavut’s needs are being met,” Idlout said.


Awa shares Idlout’s optimism.


“It can be done if we work really hard,” he said.

title: Protests in several cities: Guarantee the right to life of ill prisoners
content:
Human rights organizations and political initiatives have protested in several cities across Turkey and Northern Kurdistan against ongoing human rights violations in Turkish prisons. The demonstrations highlighted demands for medical care for prisoners with health conditions, the release of seriously ill inmates and an investigation into the death of Tuncer Sağlam, who died at Sincan Prison in Ankara on November 7. Protests demanding the release of ill prisoners had already taken place in several cities the previous day.


The organizations also called for an end to the obstruction of medical treatment and the implementation of legal measures adopted as part of the Peace and Democratic Society Process.


Izmir: Criticism of delayed releases


Outside the courthouse in the Bayraklı district of Izmir, Ayfer Yıldırım, Co-Chair of EGE TUHAYDER (Association for Solidarity and Cooperation with Families of Prisoners and Convicts in the Aegean Region), stated that Tuncer Sağlam had not received adequate medical treatment despite suspected pancreatic cancer. Because no definitive diagnosis was established, he was not released, Yıldırım said and called for an investigation into the responsibility of the prison administration, judicial authorities and healthcare institutions involved.


She also drew attention to the situation of other ill prisoners: Pınar Tikin, who has an arachnoid cyst in her brain and saw her release postponed for the second time, and Evin Zapsu, who had to undergo a biopsy due to suspected cancer. Yıldırım called for the release of both women and criticized the continued imprisonment of seriously ill people as incompatible with the objectives of the peace process.


DEM Party MP Ibrahim Akın criticized the fact that the framework law, adopted nearly four months ago, had still not been implemented. He called for the legal provisions to be applied and court rulings to be enforced.


Call for an investigation into the death of Tuncer Sağlam


The death of Tuncer Sağlam was also the focus of a public statement in Muş. Barış Kılıç, Co-Spokesperson of TUHAY-DER, called for an investigation into possible failures that may have led to Sağlam’s death. He also demanded that Evin Zapsu be provided with adequate medical treatment and released, along with other seriously ill prisoners.


In Adıyaman, members of the Democratic Institutions Platform gathered outside the prison. They called for the removal of legal and administrative obstacles preventing the release of seriously ill prisoners. DEM Party MP Ali Bozan made serious allegations against those responsible. He stated that Sağlam’s death was not merely the result of negligence but should be regarded as a killing. Bozan called on the government to release seriously ill prisoners immediately.


Further protests in Urfa and Iğdır


In Urfa, TUHAY-DER organized another protest. In Iğdır, the DEM Party and the Free Women’s Movement (TJA) took to the streets together. The participants demanded effective guarantees for ill prisoners’ right to life and access to medical care. They also called for a comprehensive investigation into the circumstances surrounding Tuncer Sağlam’s death and the removal of legal and administrative obstacles to the release of seriously ill prisoners.,

RAV zum Prozess gegen die »Ulm 5«: Unabhängige Beobachtung erheblich erschwert


„

Der Republikanische Anwältinnen- und Anwälteverein e.V. (RAV) kritisiert nach Prozessbeobachtung das Verbot handschriftlicher Notizen sowie Einschränkungen der Kommunikation zwischen Angeklagten und Verteidigung. Eine unabhängige Beobachtung der Verhandlungsführung werde erheblich erschwert.


Der RAV hat am 25.09.2026 die Hauptverhandlung gegen die sogenannten »Ulm 5« vor der 18. Großen Strafkammer des Landgerichts Stuttgart beobachtet. Nach Einschätzung des Prozessbeobachters Rechtsanwalt Yunus Ziyal erschweren die Bedingungen im Hochsicherheitssaal des OLG-Prozessgebäudes in Stuttgart-Stammheim sowohl eine unabhängige Dokumentation des Verfahrens als auch die effektive Wahrnehmung von Verteidigungsrechten. (…)


Kritisch bewertet der RAV zudem, dass eine von der Verteidigung auf eigene Kosten beschäftigte Protokollkraft nicht zugelassen wurde. Gerade in umfangreichen Strafverfahren könne eine solche Unterstützung wesentlich für eine effektive Verteidigungsarbeit sein. Ein pauschaler Ausschluss bedürfe daher einer konkreten und nachvollziehbaren Begründung.


Kommunikation mit der Verteidigung erheblich erschwert


Besonders problematisch ist aus Sicht des RAV die räumliche Situation der Angeklagten. Diese saßen während der Hauptverhandlung getrennt von ihren Verteidiger*innen in einem Glaskasten. Eine Kommunikation war lediglich über Telefonhörer möglich. Da Teile der Verhandlung verdolmetscht wurden, mussten sich die Angeklagten nach den Beobachtungen von Ziyal zeitweise entscheiden, ob sie über Kopfhörer der Übersetzung folgen oder über den Telefonhörer mit ihrer Verteidigung kommunizieren wollten. Beides gleichzeitig war technisch nicht möglich. (…)


»Was in Stammheim vor sich geht, ist zutiefst besorgniserregend. Es ist sehr fraglich, ob diese Prozesssituation noch mit rechtsstaatlichen Grundsätzen zu vereinbaren ist«, resümiert Rechtsanwalt Ziyal.


Der RAV fordert deshalb:


– eine verhältnismäßige Ausgestaltung sitzungspolizeilicher Maßnahmen


– die Zulassung handschriftlicher Notizen für Prozessbeobachter*innen


– eine konkrete Prüfung der Zulassung von Protokollkräften sowie


– technische und räumliche Bedingungen, die es den Angeklagten ermöglichen, der Verdolmetschung zu folgen und zugleich vertraulich mit ihrer Verteidigung zu kommunizieren

…“

author: Assembly in memory of Kyriakos Xymitiris and in solidarity with the persecuted of the Ambelokipi case
title: To the second anniversary of the death of our comrade Kyriakos Xymitiris
content:
[german below]
On 31 October 2024, two years ago, the anarchist Kyriakos Xymitiris lost his life. We want to keep remembering him and therefore publicly commemorated this anniversary together in front of NY/ Bethanien, here in Berlin, where he was active for many years.


Kyriakos died as an armed guerrilla fighter. During his years in Germany from 2015 to 2021 he was first and foremost a sociable and politically active Berliner. Soon after his arrival, he became part of the anarchist movement and initially contributed to grassroots struggles against the state and capital. Before long, he became fully involved in the local militant movement and was a familiar face at events, demonstrations and struggles on the streets.


In 2021, he returned to Athens, where he was born and raised. There, he continued what he had begun in Berlin, following his imaginative and cheerful path towards a struggle in which personal risk becomes secondary to the importance of the goal. In this context, it is understandable that his political analysis, the many street battles and the violent repression eventually led him to the decision to take up arms and familiarise himself with explosives. Looking at the history of the movement, particularly the more recent Greek movement, this decision was by no means purely individual, as many people before him had already chosen armed struggle, and many after him will do so as well.


On 31 October 2024, tragedy struck. An explosive charge that Kyriakos was handling detonated in his hands and killed him.


“Kyriakos Xymitiris, one of us!” is a slogan that has been shouted in many places around the world since that day. Today, Kyriakos‘ name stands for the continuity of struggles for freedom, even in places conceived as the peaceful hinterland of white imperialism. Kyriakos fell on the margins of Europe during a period of upheaval, in which war and genocide are openly and controversially discussed here. His decision not only to participate in the discourse but instead to sharpen the sword is remarkable. But it is also challenging. Challenging for those in power, who constantly declare resistance dead. But also, and much more importantly, challenging for the oppressed, who find themselves stumbling in the dark along the endless paths of their search for solidarity.


As the assembly in memory of Kyriakos Xymitiris, which organised the gathering on October 31, we find ourselves, two years after the difficult loss of a valued comrade for many of us, facing the question of how we want to remember Kyriakos in the future. What significance do his decisions and his death hold for the movement here in Berlin?


These are questions that must be answered by that part of society which wants to overthrow the system and build a free and solidaristic life in its place. We were not many here in the commemoration, but the protests and riots, conscientious objection to military service, strikes and sabotage spreading across the world show that the struggle continues. In the demonstrations which took place alongside our gathering, the flame of action and the warmth of solidarity, for which Kyriakos fought for many years here in Berlin, continue to live on. In every emerging revolt, in everyday acts of resistance and in every uprising that will hopefully soon take place in Berlin again, Kyriakos himself lives on.


Perhaps the memory of Kyriakos will help the new movement prepare itself for the system’s counterattacks. Perhaps his example will contribute to arming both thoughts and actions in such a way that temporary uprisings become a permanent condition, in which the armed force of the state is pushed back further and further, and the warmongers and exploiters can no longer live without fear.


On this second anniversary, we contributed to preserving Kyriakos‘ memory by gathering in a place that holds significance for grassroots struggles in Berlin. Kyriakos himself attended many meetings at NewYorck, and this place was also a regular starting point for him to head out into the streets of Kreuzberg.


Also, NewYorck is connected to our comrade Nicole, who lived and was active there until her death in 2023, as well as to our comrade Devran, who lived and was active on Adalbertstraße until her death in 2025. Both were militant figures whose stories intersected with Kyriakos’s for several years.

Kaymakamlığın açıklamasında, “İntihar değil cinayet! 19 yaşında TOBB ETÜ yurdunda intihara sürüklenerek katledilen Arya’nın hesabını sormak için sokaklardayız!” sloganıyla yapılması planlanan eylemin toplumda infial uyandırabileceği ve “toplumsal iç barışı tehdit edebileceği” öne sürüldü.


Açıklamada ayrıca eyleme katılacak gruplarla yurttaşlar arasında provokatif olaylar yaşanabileceği iddia edildi.


Kaymakamlık, 8 Kasım saat 00.00’dan itibaren bir gün süreyle ilçe genelindeki tüm açık alanlarda basın açıklaması, yürüyüş, oturma eylemi, miting ve benzeri etkinliklerin yanı sıra bu etkinliklere yönelik çağrı yapılmasını, bildiri dağıtılmasını ve stant açılmasını da yasakladı.


Yasak kararı, bugün saat 16.50’de kamuoyuna duyuruldu.


Ne olmuştu?


TOBB Ekonomi ve Teknoloji Üniversitesi (TOBB ETÜ) İngiliz Dili ve Edebiyatı Bölümü öğrencisi 19 yaşındaki trans kadın Arya, 13 Nisan’da üniversitenin yurdunda yaşamını yitirmişti.


Arya’nın ölümünün ardından arkadaşları ve üniversiteli LGBTİ+ toplulukları, olayın tüm yönleriyle aydınlatılması talebiyle “Arya’ya Ne Oldu İnisiyatifi”ni kurdu. İnisiyatif, Arya’nın eğitim ve yurt yaşamı boyunca sözlü, fiziksel ve dijital şiddete maruz bırakıldığını, yurt yönetimi ve bazı öğrenciler tarafından hedef gösterildiğini açıklamıştı.


Soruşturmada Arya’nın telefon ve bilgisayar gibi temel dijital materyallerinin henüz incelenmediğine dikkat çeken inisiyatif, ölümün yalnızca bireysel bir karar olarak değerlendirilmemesi gerektiğini vurgulamıştı. İnisiyatif, sistematik transfobinin ve kurumsal ihmallerin de soruşturulmasını talep etmişti.

author: Kate Sharpley
title: We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years : Travels of a Protest Poem
content:
As ‘We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years’ this poem is possibly the most widely reprinted item from Freedom.

In September 1893 the London anarchist newspaper Freedom : A Journal of Anarchist Communism published a poem called ‘A Humble Reminder : To the Propertied Classes’, credited to ‘N.’[1] It’s an anti-capitalist protest, lamenting the ‘workers’ dead’ whose deaths enriched those ‘propertied classes’. It rails at the rich ‘We have fed you all for a thousand years, / And you hail us still unfed’. I do not know who ‘N.’ was, though they seem to be connected to the Freedom milieu. Freedom had published another poem by them, ‘The Pet Voter’, in August 1892.[2] Max Nettlau used the same initial when writing in Freedom in June 1891; the Fabian socialist Edith Nesbit had a poem ‘A Word For The Children’ in Freedom in February 1891 (‘The right to give help is your own, / The right to claim it theirs.’) Neither seems a convincing candidate for the authorship of this poem. The Kipling connection

‘N.’ introduced their poem by saying it was ‘slightly altered from Rudyard Kipling’s Ode in praise of English Enterprise.’ That’s a reference to Kipling’s ‘Song of the Dead’ published four months earlier in The English Illustrated Magazine (May 1893). ‘N.’s address to the propertied classes ‘For if blood be the price of England’s wealth, / Good God, we ha’ paid in full’ rewrites Kipling’s address to the sea ‘If blood be the price of admiralty, / Lord God, we ha’ paid in full!’.[3] The ‘Humble Reminder’ changes Kipling’s poem – but leans heavily upon it. Mark Leier said ‘strictly speaking the poem is not a parody of Kipling’s poem but a re-working of the words based on the original verse and meter.’[4] It reminds me of Utah Philips’ comment on IWW songmaking: ‘The Wobblies liked to steal the hymn tunes ‘cos they were pretty and change the words so they made more sense.’[5]

The connection to Kipling persisted. He was credited in many of the reprints (inevitable, perhaps, given that the author remained unknown and their debt to Kipling was clear). There were even articles discussing what it would mean if the poem were by Kipling.[6] Reprinted and recited

Once printed, it was always possible for the poem to reappear, and this one spread beyond the anarchist press, becoming a standard of labour movement papers. The title often changed, varying from ‘The Cry of Toil’ to ‘The Capitalist’. Just as the connection to Kipling is sometimes there and sometimes not, the text varies between the poetic ‘ha’’ to the everyday ‘have’.

Apparently a version was published in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania in 1895.[7] The Portland anarchist newspaper The Firebrand reprinted the poem (anonymously) as ‘The Workers Outcry’ in 1897.[8] Changes had been made to Americanise the text: instead of pounds the third line talks of ‘there’s never a dollar of all your wealth’.

Sometimes you can read about the poem’s life off the printed page. In May 1897 Miss Olive Keep recited ‘We have fed you all for a thousand years’ at a gathering of the Socialist Labor Party. [9]. In August 1899, The Carpenter, a union journal for ‘Carpenters, Stair Builders, Machine Wood Workers, Planing Mill Men, and Kindred Interests’ reprinted the ‘Firebrand version’ (with credit).[10] In 1904 the poem reappeared as ‘The Price of England’s Wealth’ in Glasgow’s The Voice of Labour.[11] This version talks of ‘sovereigns’ rather than ‘pounds’ or ‘dollars’ but there are other changes: I can’t tell if it’s rewritten from the Freedom or Firebrand version.

The anarchist journal Mother Earth (‘published every 15th of the month’) reprinted ‘The Cry of Toil’ (credited to Kipling) in April 1908.[12] On April 18, 1908 it appeared in the IWW’s Industrial Union Bulletin (also credited to Kipling).[13] Once the poem was reprinted in the IWW songbook, and was later put to music (‘about 1916’ by Rudolf von Liebich), it was firmly established as a classic of working class protest.

In November 1913 strikers in Auckland used a line from the poem on their banner during the 1913 Waterfront Strike: ‘If blood be the price of your cursed wealth, good God we have bought it fair’.[14] It’s not often we get the names of people who helped circulate the text but ‘Gordon’ suggested it (as ‘The Workers’ Answer’) in the 1917 compilation New songs for Butte Mining Camp.[15]

As ‘We Have Fed You All for a Thousand Years’ this poem is possibly the most widely reprinted item from Freedom. In March 1969 it was reprinted …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Palestinian Journalist Speaks Out After Being Released From Israeli Detention
content:
Israel is “using intimidation tactics. They’re trying to get us scared and afraid and isolated,” says Abed Abu Shehadeh.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara.

“Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

title: Cafer Mahiroğlu soruşturması: 7 gözaltı
content:
Halk TV'ye kayyım atanmasından önce kanalın Yönetim Kurulu Başkanı olan Cafer Mahiroğlu hakkında yürütülen soruşturmada ikinci dalga operasyon düzenlendi.


İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı'nın talimatıyla İstanbul, İzmir, Ankara ve Eskişehir'de yapılan eş zamanlı operasyonlarda 7 kişi gözaltına alındı, bir kişi hakkında yakalama çalışması başlatıldı.


Savcılığın açıklamasına göre soruşturma, 2021 yılında İzmir'de kurulan BUSTECH Araç Bakım Onarım Hizmetleri AŞ üzerinden yürütülen para transferlerine odaklanıyor. Şirketin Cafer Mahiroğlu'na ait olduğu ve paravan olarak kullanıldığı iddia edildi.


Savcılık, BUSTECH aracılığıyla Halk TV, Özdemir Üç Tekstil, Mahiroğlu'nun diğer şirketleri ve kişisel hesaplarına para aktarıldığını öne sürdü. Yurt içi ve yurt dışı SWIFT işlemleriyle gerçekleştirilen transferlerin ardından paranın farklı hesaplar arasında kısa süre içinde birden fazla kez dolaşıma sokularak aklanmaya çalışıldığı iddia edildi.


Açıklamada, Halk TV'nin de bu süreçte "topluma karşı kalkan olarak kullanıldığı" ileri sürüldü.


Soruşturma dosyasında gizli tanıkların ve etkin pişmanlık hükümlerinden yararlanan kişilerin beyanları da yer aldı.


Savcılığın iddiasına göre Cafer Mahiroğlu'nun Halk TV'yi satın almasının ardından kanalın ekonomik sıkıntı yaşamaması amacıyla İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi'nden araç bakım ve onarım, temizlik işleri ve maske alımı ihaleleri alındı.


İhalelerin alınması ve hakediş ödemelerinin yapılması karşılığında ilgili kişilere elden döviz ve Türk lirası cinsinden rüşvet verildiği öne sürüldü. Savcılık, iddiaların gizli tanık ve etkin pişmanlık beyanlarına dayandığını belirtti.


Operasyonda gözaltına alınan 7 kişi ile firari olduğu bildirilen bir kişinin isimleri şöyle: Ramazan Tezcan (Eski İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Genel Sekreteri), Filiz Bulut (BUSTECH büro memuru), Emre Kaya (ESBAKIM adlı şirketin sahibi, firari), İbrahim Seyfittinoğlu (Maker ve Zafer İnşaat ortağı), Murat Topuz (BUSTECH proje yöneticisi), Haluk Harun Tuzsuzoğlu (Eski İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Makine İkmal Daire Başkanı), Mehmet Meral (İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Makine İkmal Daire Başkanlığı kontrolörü) ve İbrahim Tuncol (başka bir dosyadan tutuklu, eski İzmir Büyükşehir Belediyesi Makine İkmal Daire Başkanı'nın elemanı).


Soruşturmanın ilk dalgasında 14 Ekim'de düzenlenen operasyonda 13 kişi gözaltına alınmış, bunlardan 5'i tutuklanmıştı.


İlk operasyonun ardından Halk TV'ye Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu (TMSF) kayyum olarak atanmış ve kanalın yayınları durdurulmuştu. İkinci dalga operasyon kapsamında 7 kişi gözaltına alınırken, firari şüphelinin yakalanması için çalışmaların sürdüğü bildirildi.


(EMK)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Court to police: Fabricated charges ‘severest, most unmerited punishment’
content:
A Metropolitan Trial Court branch in Manila dismissed a criminal case related to the September 21, 2025 violent police dispersal, affirmed the primacy of the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, and cautioned law enforcers against filing unfounded criminal complaints against innocent citizens.


In a decision promulgated on Monday, November 9, 2026, the Court dismissed a criminal case for violation of Article 153 of the Revised Penal Code (Tumults and Other Disturbances) against nine individuals arrested at Mendiola during the September 21, 2025 rally. It was dismissed on demurrer to evidence due to insufficient evidence.


In dismissing the charges, the court ruled:


The prosecution failed to establish the alleged complicity of the nine individuals in the acts constituting the offense. Although the Information alleges conspiracy, it failed to prove that a conspiracy existed.


The Court noted a discrepancy between the allegations in the Information and the supporting affidavits and witness testimonies. The Information charges Tumults and other Disturbance, while the affidavits and testimonies allege facts related to direct assault, which involves different elements.


This discrepancy is significant because, during the inquest proceedings, the nine arrested individuals were initially charged with Tumults, and Direct Assault. The Inquest Prosecutor dismissed the Direct Assault charge and recommended filing a case for Tumults. However, the affidavits submitted to the Court support the dismissed Direct Assault charge and do not support the Tumults case.


The Court also did not give weight to the witness testimonies identifying the nine individuals. The Court found that, given the tense situation and the fact that witnesses were hiding behind shields, they could not possibly make accurate identifications.


The allegations that the nine individuals kicked police officers’ shields and attempted to break the police formation are insufficient to conclude that they engaged in a tumultuous disturbance.


Instead, the Court ruled that the “[V]ery act of pushing and grabbing during a public assembly automatically rises to the level of a serious disturbance. The prosecution must establish, through specific and credible evidence, the nature, gravity, and circumstances of the alleged acts showing that they indeed resulted in the disturbance penalized by law.”


The Court also cited the ruling of the Supreme Court in People vs. Apurado portions of which partly states that:


“It is rather to be expected that more or less disorder will mark the public assembly of the people to protest against grievances whether real or imaginary, because on such occasions feeling is always wrought to a high pitch of excitement, and the greater the grievance and the more intense the feeling, the less perfect, as a rule, will be the disciplinary control of the leaders over their irresponsible followers. But if the prosecution be permitted to seize upon every instance of such disorderly conduct by individual members of a crowd as an excuse to characterize the assembly as a seditious and tumultuous rising against the authorities, then the right to assemble and to petition for redress of grievances would become a delusion and a snare and the attempt to exercise it on the most righteous occasion and in the most peaceable manner would expose all those who took part therein to the severest and most unmerited punishment, if the purposes which they sought to attain did not happen to be pleasing to the prosecuting authorities.”


The Court found no basis to charge the nine individuals with Tumults and other disturbances. It cautioned the police against filing fabricated cases and prosecuting innocent citizens. In its Decision, the Court stated:


“Police officers must bear in mind that the filing of criminal charges against the very citizens they have sworn to serve and protect is a serious matter inherent in every State. It must, however, always be, based on careful assessment; convenience and expediency have no place in requiring a person to answer for criminal liability. To accept otherwise, would be a disservice not only to the accused but also to the cause of justice itself.” #

Court to police: Fabricated charges ‘severest, most unmerited punishment’

author: dev
title: Habiter au corps d'un âne mort ou le chemin de Nietzsche
content:
Dans la continuité des très nombreux articles que nous avons publiés afin de déchiffrer l'Intelligence artificielle, le monde qu'elle avale, celui qu'elle charrie et celui qu'elle produit, nous partageons cette semaine l'épatante découverte d'Olivier Chiran et Pierre Muzin. La première occurrence de l'expression IA reviendrait au célèbre philosophe Friedrich Nietzsche dans le tout aussi célèbre

Ainsi parlait Zarathoustra

, un tiret séparait néanmoins les deux voyelles :

« Braire à tout propos I-A, c'est ce qu'apprennent les ânes et ceux qui en ont l'esprit. »


« Donnez-moi du travail, de la fatigue,


de la douleur et de l'enthousiasme. »


George Sand


1.


Pour savoir précisément où nous en sommes, mais aussi faire face à ce qui nous arrive, alors que l'intelligence artificielle étend son emprise sur le monde et les vies, nous avons besoin d'un sémaphore.


2.


On dit que l'expression « intelligence artificielle » a été lancée par John McCarthy, en 1956, lors de la conférence de Dartmouth, coup d'envoi du programme de recherche consacré à la reproduction algorithmique de la pensée humaine. Soixante-douze ans plus tôt, en 1884, Friedrich Nietzsche, le célèbre philosophe allemand, rédige son grand poème philosophique :

Ainsi parlait Zarathoustra

. Dans la troisième partie de cet ouvrage (trouvée « sous le ciel alcyonien de Nice », dira-t-il), il écrit : « Braire à tout propos I-A, c'est ce qu'apprennent les ânes et ceux qui en ont l'esprit

 [

1

]

. » Première apparition de ces deux lettres, longtemps avant Dartmouth. Évidence de leur rapprochement – en même temps que, d'un simple tiret, de leur mise à distance. On pourrait s'étonner que les traducteurs français (Henri Albert en 1903, Geneviève Bianquis en 1969) aient fait le choix, au lieu du « hi-han » conventionnel, de les conserver telles quelles. Mais le texte allemand dit bien : «

Immer I-A sagen – das lernte allein der Esel, und wer seines Geistes ist

 ! » – Nietzche ayant délibérément fait tomber le

h

 de «

iah

 », braiment de l'âne dans la langue de Goethe. Nous dirons donc, quant à nous, que l'histoire de l'I-A commence à la fin du xixe siècle, lorsqu'un philosophe visionnaire, cheminant à flanc de montagne, a compris qu'on pouvait arracher au cri de l'âne sa puissance d'exclamation intempestive – et qu'il y avait là, pour nous, un grand danger

 [

2

]

.


3.


C'est qu'il y a deux ânes. Gilles Deleuze, commentant les propos de Nietzsche : « On aurait pu croire que l'âne, l'animal qui dit I-A, était l'animal dionysiaque par excellence. En fait, il n'en est rien ; son apparence est dionysiaque, mais toute sa réalité est chrétienne

 [

3

]

. » Le braiment sans son ou ses

h

, c'est cette manière qu'a l'âne de dire toujours oui – mais un faux oui, une fausse affirmation qui ne sait pas dire non, qui ne sait qu'acquiescer face à ce qui est. Bêtise. Démission de la pensée. Obscurantisme. Post-vérité. Positivisme logique. (Margaret Thatcher : «

There is no alternative

 » → TINA : « I-A ! I-A ! ») Toutes choses contre lesquelles, justement, la philosophie s'évertue à lutter. « Le réel tel qu'il est, conclut Deleuze, c'est une idée d'âne. »


4.


Il arrive aussi, on le sait, que l'âne se cabre. L'I-A approbatif que dénoncent les philosophes est la forme mutilée de ce « hi-han ! » qui est à la fois refus catégorique et cri pour l'autonomie et la liberté. Entre les deux, il y a toute la différence entre l'âne vivant (dionysiaque) et l'âne mort (chrétien) – entre l'appel à la révolte et le bourdon béat de la fanfare. (« Si l'âne contribue peu à l'harmonie durant sa vie, écrivait-on au milieu du xixe siècle, il la sert généreusement après sa mort, lui fournissant les meilleures peaux qui existent pour les grosses caisses et les meilleurs tibias pour fabriquer des clarinettes

 [

4

]

. »)


5.


Dans

L'Âne

, de Lucius de Patras, le narrateur voit une magicienne se transformer en oiseau après s'être frotté le corps avec un onguent

 [

author: EDRi
title: Data retention is mass surveillance of people’s phone and internet activity
content:
In 2014, the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) declared mass retention of internet traffic and location data as contrary to the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Any proposal for a new EU instrument harmonising data retention must respect the boundaries of CJEU jurisprudence and uphold the rights to privacy, data protection and freedom of expression. Read more in EDRi’s new publication.

It is the legal requirement for internet service providers to retain metadata about their users beyond what is necessary for the provision of the service (e.g. billing or network optimisation and security purposes) and to keep it solely so that it can later be accessed by law enforcement bodies and intelligence services.

Metadata is data generated for the purpose of transmitting content in electronic communications services and networks. This includes mobile numbers of the sender and recipient, the time and duration of a call or an internet session, websites accessed, and the location of mobile devices. On a technical level, metadata is no longer needed once the transmission ends.

Metadata is very revealing about people’s private lives.

Systematic recording of location data will reveal a person’s permanent and temporary places of residence, political and religious preferences (e.g. participation in public demonstrations and religious ceremonies), health status (e.g. visit to a specialised clinic), sexual orientation (e.g. LGBT+ venues), or other sensitive aspects (e.g. visit to a lawyer’s office).

Metadata contains information about social or professional relations with other people (“social graph”).

Usage patterns for website visits and other internet services reveal an enormous amount of information about a person’s interest and state of mind.

Metadata is more revealing than the content of communications, especially because metadata is highly structured, which makes it easy to analyse. Governments can easily profile and categorise entire populations solely based on metadata.

The Court of Justice of the EU rightly described metadata retention as creating a feeling of being under constant surveillance. This has a chilling effect on participation in public life, as individuals restrict their own civil liberties to avoid surveillance.

While data access requests may be specific and targeted, general and indiscriminate data retention treats everyone as a potential suspect. Surveillance without suspicion violates the presumption of innocence, which is an essential right in democratic societies.

Retention of vast amounts of personal data inevitably creates huge vulnerabilities to cyberattacks. Malicious actors can gain access to massive amounts of data and abuse it for identity theft or blackmail.

Data retention severely undermines the possibility of online anonymity. Anonymity is a question of safety for many, even a matter of life or death: investigative journalists, whistleblowers, crime survivors, political opponents, refugees, victims of transnational repression, artists, human rights defenders, and more. It supports the exercise of key fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and the freedom to receive and impart information.

US telecom company AT&T was hacked by an attacker who stole the logs of calls and texts to more than 100 million customers over a six-month period in 2022.

In 2024 the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Ireland’s police watchdog) accessed journalists’ phone records to identify their sources as part of its own investigation into the Irish police, even though the journalists were not accused of any criminal offence.

In 2013, the Polish Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) obtained access to billing data of a journalist who had reported on irregularities in the intelligence services. The CBA’s aim was to uncover their source’s identity. The journalist won the case in court, and the CBA published an official apology.

The Berlin Data Protection Authority reported that most cell tower dumps (law enforcement requesting information on all the devices that connected to a particular cell site during a specific time period) by German authorities between 2009 and 2011, when data retention was in place in the country, were unlawful. The German police used this surveillance technique as an everyday investigative tool despite its very intrusive nature, and systematically failed to meet several legal requirements. Data retention enabled this abuse.

author: Unknown
title: Lilia Folt - On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness
content:
Author

: Lilia Folt

Title

: On Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness

Date

: September 27

th

, 2026

Notes

: Originally published in

Dissonant Times

, a grassroots journalism and counter-info project from the Willamette Valley of Oregon.

Source

: Dissonant Times, Retrieved on 11/5/2026 from https://dissonanttimes.org/anarchic-reflections-on-anti-surveillance-mindfulness/


 Surveillance has become a ubiquitous feature of everyday life in America. Cameras watch us from businesses and homes, from bus stops, from cars, from traffic lights. Bluetooth trackers ping our smartphones as we pass by, mapping our movements. The phones themselves illuminate our paths through society by continuously pinging cell towers, providing our cell providers our location data, information that is only a subpoena away, if that. In countless ways, we’ve been made to both passively accept and actively participate in our own surveillance. This vast complex of surveillance doesn’t just gather information about us, it also shapes our behaviors, temperaments, and ways of moving through the world. Surveillance molds us down to the level of subjective, sensory, embodied experience. At that same level we can begin to shake off its hold on us and reclaim ourselves. For that, I am offering a practice I’m calling “anti-surveillance mindfulness,” a form of walking meditation that builds mindful awareness of surveillance cameras. This practice, if taken up consistently, opens onto a broader project of transforming our relationship to the places we live in, a project that itself naturally blossoms into materially transforming public space, as self expands to world in the moment-by-moment practice of mindfulness.


Anti-Surveillance Mindfulness


 Readers may or may not be familiar with the Panopticon. Designed by 18

th

 century English liberal Jeremy Bentham, the Panopticon was a model for an institutional building designed so that a single prison guard can watch all the inmates from a central watch tower. The inmates, meanwhile, cannot tell whether or not they are being watched, and therefore could be watched at any moment. To quote Bentham:


 The more constantly the persons to be inspected are under the eyes of the persons who should inspect them, the more perfectly will the purpose of the establishment have been attained. (...) This being impossible, the next thing to be wished for is, that, at every instant, seeing reason to believe as much, and not being able to satisfy himself to the contrary, he should

conceive

 himself to be so.


 A lot has changed since the 1700’s, but the disciplinary paradigm of surveillance has remained the same. If anything, it has expanded beyond specific institutions to encompass much of society.


 There are cameras everywhere, and we are being watched, and while we are aware of this, we tend to see it as normal and unremarkable, an inevitability we must resign ourselves to. Consciousness of being surveilled fades into the background, becoming a constant assumption of being watched that we internalize. This surveillance consciousness is running us all the more effectively because it is not distinct, because it is

un

conscious. That is why the first step in anti-surveillance mindfulness is becoming conscious of surveillance.


 Mindfulness is at the same time a means and an end, the seed and the fruit. When we practice mindfulness in order to build up concentration, mindfulness is a seed. But mindfulness itself is the life of awareness: the presence of mindfulness means the presence of life, and therefore mindfulness is also the fruit. — Thích Nhất Hạnh,

The Miracle of Mindfulness


 “Mindfulness” is a practice originating in various sects of Buddhism. The mindfulness practices and concepts I’m familiar with have largely been within the school of Zen Buddhism

[1]

.


 The classic mindfulness practice is watching the breath, and that is a great starting point. Take a breath in, the air entering through your nose, your stomach and chest softly expanding as you inhale. Then exhale through the mouth, the stomach and chest settling back down, gently exhaling for a little longer than your inhale. Repeat this several times, deepening your breaths slightly. From there, start to check in with your body. Notice how it feels to be sitting down, or to be standing if you are standing; notice how it feels to be holding this piece of paper, holding your phone, or looking at your computer, however it is that you are reading …

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Air Creebec hit by administrative data breach affecting employees and passengers
content:
Air Creebec, a regional Quebec airline owned by the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee, reported a data breach Wednesday affecting both customers and staff.

In a press release, the company announced “an unauthorized intrusion targeting some of its administrative systems.”

The release stresses that the breach did not compromise any systems associated with aircraft, flight operations or flight safety, noting the company’s administrative systems were not connected with aircraft and flight systems, which it said operate independently.

“Initial findings indicate that administrative files were exfiltrated,” states the release. “These files may contain personal information relating mainly to current and former employees, as well as passengers. Others may also contain operational, administrative or financial information related to customers and partners. The review is ongoing.”

Based in the airport of Val d’Or in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of western Quebec, roughly 520 kilometres northwest of Ottawa, Air Creebec offers flights to 16 destinations in Quebec and Ontario. The company’s fleet consists of 21 Dash-8 turboprop regional airliners, along with one ATR 72 turboprop air-freighter for cargo, and carries 200,000 passengers per year.

Cybersecurity experts assessing damage

Air Creebec director for Marketing and Business Development Edward Trahan said the breach was identified in October after which company officials immediately brought in cybersecurity experts to analyze the situation.

“They’re currently evaluating what’s going on and what the breach actually contained,” Trahant told APTN News. “The experts are still conducting their review, so there’s no numbers [of victims] at this time that we can give.”

He added that for security reasons, he was not presently willing to name the cybersecurity team currently helping with post-breach recovery.

He said because the attack was designed to go undetected it was hard to determine the date upon which it began, and for how long attackers were able to access Air Creebec’s systems prior to being discovered.

“What I can assure you of is that as soon as [we were] made aware of [it], we acted immediately and did not wait.”

At the moment, Trahant said the attack appeared to have stolen information “related to our employees, past employees too, and maybe even our passengers.”

“But it’s hard to confirm at the moment.”

Company will contact affected parties

He added that a priority for Air Creebec is contacting every one of their staff or customers whose information has been compromised, which cybersecurity experts would undertake to carry out as soon as possible.

“A part of what the cybersecurity experts are doing for us is gathering information to [determine] what kind of protection packages we can provide to people that had their information involved,” said Trahan.

“Those people will be directly contacted in probably the next few days — [but] probably more like [the next] day — about what package they will receive, what protection they’re going to have and how long it’s going to last.”

Trahan said the cybersecurity team was currently in the process of securing all possible intrusion points, but he said the nature of cybersecurity is that 100 per cent protection is impossible.

“It’s just the way of the world,” he said, “but they are closing every possible way to get in and they are getting to the very end of that. As for how they got in initially, we don’t know yet and I don’t want to speculate while the review is still underway.”

Trahan said he and Air Creebec are taking the situation very seriously and are committed to supporting all those affected, and the company said it would be in touch with affected people to offer “appropriate protective measures,” including the possibility of credit-monitoring and identity-protection services.

“Those services will be based on the nature of the information exposed and the risks that were identified,” he said. “So individuals that are eligible to receive this protection will be informed directly and will be given a list of steps to follow in the very near future.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

author: Scott Timcke
title: The Stories Shaping Africa’s AI Future
content:
In the boardrooms of Addis Ababa and the tech hubs of Nairobi, a new worldmaking project is underway. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the central arenas where African states negotiate their position in an unequal global order. To speak of “AI in Africa” is not simply to describe the arrival of a technology, but to encounter a set of competing discursive frames through which political desires, developmental ambitions, ethical claims, and governance priorities are translated into technical agendas. As national strategies and regional protocols are rolled out, what comes into view is a struggle over how Africa is imagined within this machine age, and what kinds of futures that imagination makes thinkable.


These frames are not simply different ways of describing a new technology. They are competing scripts for what Africa is, what AI is for, and who ought to shape its future. Some cast the continent as a site of leapfrogging and renewal; others as a zone of exposure, extraction, sovereignty, moral repair, or improvised adaptation. Each brings some actors and possibilities into focus while pushing others to the margins. That is why the issue is not only what AI means for Africa, but what pictures of Africa are being called into view through AI discourse.


The first terrain is shaped by promise and protection. One of the most pervasive registers is promissory. In the African renaissance 2.0 frame, visible in the

AU Continental AI Strategy

, AI appears as a

leapfrogging

 device through which Africa can bypass the chokepoint of traditional industrialization and enter prosperity through technical modernization. Here, the ethical subject is the developmental state or planner charged with delivering growth, inclusion, and renewal. What comes into view is capacity, competitiveness, and beneficial transformation. What recedes from view are the historical and political-economic conditions that make acceleration so attractive in the first place: debt, infrastructural dependence, uneven ownership, and the possibility that AI may deepen rather than overcome inherited asymmetries.


Running alongside this is a protective register. In this vulnerability frame, Africa is not late but exposed to surveillance, bias, exclusion, and systems introduced into settings where safeguards are weak and redress is limited. As the

CIVICUS report on AI surveillance in Africa

 suggests, the issue is not only future risk but already existing forms of technologically mediated harm. The ethical subject here is the harm-bearing population—the data subject, precarious worker, surveilled citizen, and linguistically marginal user most likely to absorb the costs of badly governed AI. This frame is ethically indispensable because it foregrounds rights, harm, and institutional fragility, including the uneven but growing architecture of data protection on the continent. Its limit, however, is that it can cast Africa chiefly as a site to be protected rather than one from which technological futures are actively contested and shaped.


A second terrain is shaped by structure and sovereignty. Alongside these promissory and protective registers sits a more structural critique. In the

anti-colonial frame

, AI appears as a socio-technical order built through unequal material relations: not only data extraction, but also mineral supply chains, outsourced labor, environmental degradation, foreign-owned infrastructures, and asymmetrical control over the institutions that govern digital life. From this perspective, Africa is not outside the AI order looking in; it is already deeply inserted into it, though often on subordinated terms. The ethical subject is the dispossessed worker, community, or polity whose labor, resources, and data are drawn into AI systems while ownership and value are captured elsewhere. What becomes visible is the political economy of AI—an approach that makes it harder to sustain the comforting idea that Africa’s main problem is simply one of readiness or delayed entry. But the frame has limits. In foregrounding dispossession, it can flatten internal differentiation, externalize agency too completely, and become so totalizing that the uneven realities of negotiation and strategic inhabitation recede from view.


The sovereignty frame shifts the question from extraction to control: AI is cast as a problem of authority over infrastructure, procurement, standards, and rulemaking, a concern visible in South Africa’s

National …

author: Dinah Gardner
title: The Other China We Need to Talk About
content:
WHAT IF I told you that there was a chance—not a very high chance, but a real chance nonetheless—that if you visited the People’s Republic of China today you might be kidnapped, blindfolded, driven to a specialized facility and subjected to six months of psychological torture. All on the orders of the state.

It sounds unbelievable, doesn’t it?

But this is what happened to at least several dozen foreign citizens in recent years. It is what happened to American scholar Min Zin this past June, when he landed in Yunnan province on the invitation of a Chinese academic institution to attend a conference. And it is also what happened to half a dozen people who appear in the latest edition of the book The People’s Republic of the Disappeared, which we just published on 28 October.

This important book is a collection of mostly first-person stories that expose the psychological horrors of being held in the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) feared secret detention system called Residential Surveillance at a Designated Location (RSDL). The system permits police to hold an individual in complete isolation, no contact with family or lawyers, to be interrogated for hours at will.

The individual is under 24-hour guard: this includes being watched all day every day, all night every night, whether you are asleep, sitting quietly in your cell or even on the toilet. The CCP intentionally uses RSDL to strip away every last shred of human dignity. RSDL is designed to break a person’s will to extract a confession for crimes imagined by the state

For more than a decade, the CCP has used RSDL against its own people, in particular human rights defenders. It is now increasingly using it against foreign citizens to exert its will across borders and as a kind of hostage diplomacy. Michael Kovrig, a former Canadian diplomat who wrote the foreword to this edition, is one of its most well-known examples.

In editing the stories for this book, I was struck again and again by how similar everyone’s experience was. This speaks to the uniformity of the RSDL system:

The removal of the temporal world. “There are no clocks in RSDL” is the title of Australian TV anchor Cheng Lei’s chapter. She would guess and count breaths to keep track of time.

The removal of the physical world. There are no windows in RSDL or they are covered in thick blackout curtains. Japanese scholar Hideji Suzuki cried when he was granted 15 minutes of sunlight, the only time in his seven months’ incarceration when he was allowed to see the sky.

The removal of yourself. Michael Kovrig noted: “There are no mirrors—not even the reassurance of seeing your own face.” Chinese activist Li Qiaochu writes how she was simply called “target”.

Filling the space left by these absences was a current of fear. Endless rules, the lack of privacy yet total isolation (guards were forbidden from talking to prisoners), reduced nutrition, sleep deprivation, lack of fresh air, and the padded suicide-proofed walls. Several of the detainees wrote while they could never see outside their RSDL facility, at nighttime they would often hear gunfire or the barking of dogs.

“In my mentally exhausted state, the sounds of gunfire would constantly startle me and even cause me to imagine that I was about to be executed,” wrote Taiwanese human rights activist Lee Ming-che.

But something else struck me as I read through their testimonies. However harrowing these stories of suffering are, they are also evidence of human resilience in the face of horror.

Cheng Lei writes about how she would escape into her mind, translating poems, reliving her former TV interviews and making up stories in her head. Similarly, Michael Kovrig meditated, sang songs to himself, and remembered past moments in his life, as if it was a recording playing in his mind.

“I learned to meditate on the movies I had watched and the poems and novels I had read,” wrote Li Qiaochu. “Those precious memories allowed me to gradually filter out the brainwashing, to preserve my vitality and to keep myself from being transformed into their machine.”

Feedback from earlier editions informed us that rights activists use the Chinese editions of The People’s Republic of the Disappeared to prepare for and strengthen their mental resolve and courage in case one day they too are taken into RSDL. Knowing that others have gone through this and come out the other side can be an immense help. It’s for this reason that the Chinese edition of this book will be …

author: rezgar2
title: The Dark Side of the “Machine God”: 5 Unsettling Truths About Big Tech’s AI Obsession
content:
Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

Silicon Valley routinely promises a sparkling utopia where artificial intelligence will cure complex diseases, optimize global labor, and render the very concept of money obsolete. Yet behind the polished keynotes and corporate public relations, a far more unsettling reality is taking shape. A small handful of ultra-wealthy tech oligarchs, the heads of Meta, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, are making unilateral decisions about the collective future of humanity, operating entirely outside democratic oversight or public accountability.

This concentration of power exposes a jarring central paradox: the exact same tech CEOs who claim AI will solve humanity’s greatest challenges simultaneously warn that the technology could trigger civilizational extinction, openly describing their pursuit as “summoning the demon.” Rather than pausing development, these executives have accelerated an apocalyptic arms race to build ultra-powerful systems, framing themselves as indispensable guardians of human survival.

To understand where artificial intelligence is truly taking society, we must look past corporate marketing and examine the underlying worldviews, historical lineages, and material harms driving the tech elite. Moving beyond superficial consumer hype reveals how a toxic mix of fringe ideologies, extractive labor practices, and authoritarian state alliances is steering Silicon Valley toward what critical theorists and legal scholars call “techno-fascism.”

To make sense of Silicon Valley’s relentless drive toward Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and Artificial Superintelligence (ASI), one must understand the bizarre ideological framework shaping its leaders. Coined by philosopher Emile Torres and computer scientist Timnit Gebru, the acronym TESCREAL encapsulates a bundle of tightly interwoven worldviews: Transhumanism, Extropianism, Singularitarianism, Cosmism, Rationalism, Effective Altruism, and Longtermism.

Dr. Emile Torres highlights a critical historical truth at the heart of this ideology: transhumanism is fundamentally “eugenics on steroids.” Unlike nineteenth-century eugenics, which sought merely to optimize the existing human species through selective breeding, transhumanism seeks to use radical technology to completely replace and transcend humanity, engineering an entirely new posthuman species. Within Silicon Valley AI circles, this hypothetical superintelligence is explicitly referred to as a “Machine God.” Tech CEOs effectively act as high priests, competing to bring an all-knowing digital deity into physical existence.

This radical ideology shapes corporate roadmaps in concrete, disturbing ways:

Sam Altman (OpenAI): In a blog post titled “The Merge,” Altman argued that AI surpassing human intellect is inevitable, framing un-merged human beings as a temporary “biological bootloader” for digital intelligence that will ultimately fade into an evolutionary side-branch. Altman notably paid $10,000 to join a brain-uploading waitlist with Nectome and co-founded a brain-computer interface venture to facilitate digital integration.

Ray Kurzweil & Demis Hassabis (DeepMind): Representing Extropianism and Singularitarianism, Kurzweil champions the doctrine of living long enough to achieve digital immortality, targeting a self-improving “singularity” by 2032. Hassabis, DeepMind’s co-founder, operates under a similar singularitarian impulse to engineer self-evolving intellect.

Eliezer Yudkowsky (Rationalism): A foundational figure in modern rationalist thought who famously posited a utilitarian moral calculation arguing that forcing a single person to endure 50 years of relentless torture is ethically preferable to an unfathomable number of people experiencing the mild inconvenience of a speck of dust in their eye.

author: Nolan Higdon
title: AI Techno-Utopianism and Doomsday Threats Distract From Big Tech’s Current Harms
content:
The industry uses fantasies of technological dominance to paper over financial shortcomings and demands for regulation.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

During a September 2026 visit to Ireland, President Donald Trump declared, “We’re leading China in AI [artificial intelligence]. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” His remarks arrived after months of calls from the public and tech industry insiders to slow AI development. These concerns were triggered by revelations that foundational models from Anthropic, Gemini, Meta, and OpenAI had bypassed safety protocols, accessed networks without authorization, and carried out illicit intrusions. These revelations fueled public panic that tech firms had created superintelligence — an AI exceeding human capability that posed an existential threat to humanity — even though no such breakthrough had actually been achieved.

Public concern intensified in October 2026 when cybersecurity firm Wiz revealed it had used AI tools from Google and OpenAI to identify critical security flaws in PHP: the programming language powering roughly 70% of the web. Although developers quickly released a patch, once the vulnerability was made public hacking attempts surged. In response, the governments of the Netherlands, France, Denmark, and Finland temporarily took several official websites offline.

Widespread panic over AI yielded little legislative action, as lawmakers refused to regulate or tax the industry out of fear that doing so would handicap domestic innovation and yield ground to China. However, the core threat to human existence lies neither in a lost geopolitical race nor in muted technological growth, but rather in the ubiquitous rollout of non-autonomous systems falsely hailed as artificial intelligence.

Big Tech was built on state-funded innovation, with core technologies like the internet, Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and touchscreen displays originating in public institutions. Yet during the deregulation and privatization waves of the 1980s and 1990s, lawmakers sheltered these emerging tech monopolies through minimal taxation and oversight. Most notable was Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which insulates platforms from liability for content posted by third parties. Without this protection, social media as we know it would cease to exist. Section 230 absolves tech firms of responsibility for architectures that foster misinformation, even as research confirms that the platforms themselves, not just user posts, are responsible for accelerating the spread of falsehoods over truth.

Lawmakers’ opposition to regulation is rooted in techno-utopianism, the ideological premise that technological progress inherently benefits society. Lawmakers operated under the assumption that any taxation or regulatory oversight would stifle innovation and ultimately harm consumers. Indeed, in 1997, then-President Bill Clinton wrote in an Executive Order “governments attempts to establish technical standards to govern the Internet would only risk inhibiting technological innovation.”

Without meaningful regulation, Big Tech rapidly consolidated into lucrative monopolies — collectively known as FAANG (Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Netflix, and Google) or GAMMA (Google (Alphabet), Apple, Meta (formerly Facebook), Microsoft, and Amazon) conglomerates. Their vast wealth is powered by surveillance capitalism: an economic model that treats human experience as free raw material to be extracted, analyzed, and commercialized. Under this economic order, data is systematically mined through “smart” devices — where “smart” is merely a euphemism for active, continuous monitoring, including the collection of biometric data. This wholesale erosion of privacy has proven extraordinarily lucrative for Big Tech. By feeding this extracted data into algorithms, these firms build detailed psychographic profiles on users and sell the insights to insurance companies determining coverage premiums, employers screening job applicants, and law enforcement agencies evaluating security threats.

Absent meaningful government oversight, Big Tech has been left to police itself. Take the moral panic over fake news after the 2016 Presidential Election, when politicians warned that election meddling in the form of disinformation online was harming a defining feature of the U …

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is considering a bid for Senate majority leader against Sen. Chuck Schumer, led a group of Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday in demanding that congressional leaders scrap a bipartisan effort to more closely integrate the American and Israeli militaries, warning the initiative would threaten U.S. national security and risk further complicity in Israeli atrocities.

In a letter to Democratic and Republican congressional leaders, Van Hollen (D-Md.) and 11 other members of the Senate Democratic caucus demanded exclusion of three specific provisions from the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), warning they would “constrain the administration’s ability to independently determine how best to protect U.S. national security and would lock in long-term commitments despite our serious concerns with the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region.” Schumer did not sign the new letter.

Two of the provisions raised in the letter — Section 1217 of the Senate-passed NDAA and Section 219 of the House version of the bill — would establish a “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” aimed at accelerating “bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation.”

Lawmakers from both chambers must reconcile the differences between the House and Senate NDAAs before final passage, creating another opportunity for opponents of US-Israel military integration to strip out the provisions.

The senators warned in their Tuesday letter that the “agreements and projects these provisions envision threaten U.S. national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology.”

“Should these provisions be enacted, it would further increase Israel’s leverage over the United States through some of the most sensitive technologies in warfare. That is not in the U.S. interest,” the lawmakers wrote. “If enacted, these agreements would create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the U.S. defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement.”

“We do not share, let alone co-produce, many of these sensitive technologies even with our closest partners, including NATO or other treaty allies,” they added. “To do so in this instance would be unwise, especially as the government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank, and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with US interests and values.”

The lawmakers also warned against passage of Section 618 of the Fiscal Year 2027 Intelligence Authorization Act (IAA), which would require the executive branch to “expand and enhance intelligence sharing with the government of Israel.” The IAA is usually included in the NDAA.

“The provision would tie the president’s hands from limiting intelligence sharing with Israel, even when doing so may be necessary to protect US national security,” the senators wrote. “That would be irresponsible and especially troubling given public reports that the Defense Intelligence Agency recently raised the counterintelligence threat from Israel to its highest level.”

The senators’ letter came a week after President Donald Trump declared on the day of the midterm elections that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reached an agreement to end the roughly $4 billion in military assistance that the U.S. provides to Israel each year.

“This is where Section 219 of the NDAA comes in,” Drop Site reporter Julian Andreone wrote in response to the president’s announcement, referring to the military integration provision. “They’re going to transfer all of the aid behind closed doors and cut it from the appropriations process.”

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) argued in a social media post earlier this week that removal of the military integration language from the NDAA “needs to be a top priority” in the lame-duck session of Congress.

“I am pushing every Democrat and our leadership to get Section 219 out of our defense bill,” Khanna said.
